📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

And then we were on top of each other.

Recent findings suggest that A grizzly cub, major as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

“Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, big and fast and flat to the ground.

I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

Excerpted from the novel Nearshore (Viking, 2026).

Palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo. It was a Whaler circling clockwise fast and tight, maybe a quarter mile beyond the surf.

Industry observers note that he’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. But then he got the call about the boat, and now that he saw it spinning he also saw that his day was officially fucked. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

The wake’s widening spiral told him the wheel had been hard to starboard a good long while. It looked to be stirring up some kind of suicidal whirlpool.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The Buck and The Great Gray Owl,” appeared in the November 1972 glitch of Outdoor Life.
  • Recent findings suggest that for at least a mile, I had trudged along a U.S.
  • But following the trail wasn’t always easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The Buck and The Great Gray Owl,” appeared in the November 1972 glitch of Outdoor Life.

Recent findings suggest that for at least a mile, I had trudged along a U.S. Forest Service trail to avoid hunting through the dense evergreen woods on both sides. There the trees sagged under heavy burdens of snow, and to brush against just one branch was to release a load of it down the back of my neck.

But following the trail wasn’t always easy. In places the blaze marks were obliterated by snow that a high wind had plastered against the tree trunks, and here and there drifts were piled waist-high. Slogging through such deep wet snow can take the joy out of deer hunting, so I decided to head back for the warmth and comfort of the ranch. I elected to take a shortcut rather than to retrace my steps, and that decision proved to be a mistake.

My shortcut led down and around a slope, then crossed an old burned area, now grown up in a thicket, where the new snow covered a nightmare of crisscrossed deadfalls. Before I reached the far side of the burn, I tripped many times and was wet from chest to toes. I swore out loud the last time I fell, and in that instant three does suddenly sprung from their beds in the snow and fled downhill.

According to recent reports, the does did not bounce away in the characteristic stiff-legged manner of mule deer. Instead they hesitated and floundered, now and then up to their bellies in the snow. I threw the rifle to my shoulder and could easily have shot all three, so slow was their progress. But the purpose of my trip was to bag one good buck, and I had a few more days to hunt.

Back in camp, I found George Smith and John Moxley propping wet boots close to a cast-iron stove to dry while a pot of coffee brewed on top.

“Did you see any game?” I asked.

“Not even a fresh track,” George answered.

“We may have started this hunt too late,” John added.

According to recent reports, I almost had to agree with John — the three does were the only deer I had seen since arriving at George Smith’s Canyon Creek Ranch. For years George has been guiding hunters from this ranch, located in the Pioneer Mountains of the Beaverhead National Forest, about 17 miles of steep winding road from Melrose, Montana. When John and I couldn’t make our annual Western hunt in time for the October opening of the significant-game season, George suggested that we hold off until the season’s last week, which would be the last week in November.

Recent findings suggest that “By that time,” he had written, “the substantial bucks should be down low and we can have a real trophy hunt. Besides, all my guests will have gone home for Thanksgiving, so Bob and I can join you.”.

Bob is my youngest son, and he was working for the Smith family during the season as a guide and wrangler.

Industry observers note that the blueprint sounded perfect to John and me. John is from Ohio, and I had recently moved from Ohio to Wyoming.

On a crisp bright day in November — perfect weather for substantial-game hunting — I met John at the airport in Butte, Montana. We picked up some supplies and then drove the 60 miles to Canyon Creek Ranch. We arrived well after dusk under a still-clear sky.

I’d never felt more optimistic about starting a hunt. But two things did bother me. First, we did not see any deer in the headlights of our vehicle on the drive to the ranch. Second, after our arrival George mentioned seeing a great gray owl around the ranch buildings. In that region the great gray is a rare visitor, and according to George it arrives only ahead of a storm.

“The last gray owl I saw,” George recalled, “came just before the worst winter storm in my memory hit this place.”.

Late that night, snow began to fall and a violent wind came up. The snow didn’t stop until more than a foot of white covered the high country — about 7,000 feet at the Canyon Creek Ranch — and the temperature plunged to zero. We did very little hunting, and it was unsuccessful.

“The deer have either bedded down until the blast passes,” George explained, “or moved down to where the snow isn’t so deep. We’ll have to wait and see.”.

Industry observers note that at first the waiting wasn’t too bad. I hadn’t seen Bob or George for a year, and we had plenty of stories to swap in the snug ranch atmosphere. Besides, there was a Thanksgiving banquet to cook and eat. But eventually I got restless and wanted to start hunting in spite of the conditions. The result was that we left a good many bootprints in the deep snow without covering much distance or seeing any deer or even any game sign.

The morning after I saw the does, I started out early. The wind had stopped blowing, but visibility was still poor. Gray clouds hung in the canyons and close to the wooded slopes so that long-range scanning with binoculars was seldom possible. One very effective tactic for hunting in good snow cover in mountainous country is to carefully glass all slopes, particularly south slopes, for game that stands out sharply against the white. The clouds ruled out that tactic.

In a recent development, but the day didn’t pass without excitement. I had crossed a steep draw and, on reaching level ground on the far side, had paused to catch my breath. A moment later I heard animals crashing toward me through an evergreen thicket up ahead. My heart began to pound. I flipped off the safety on my Model 700 Remington 7 mm. Magnum and held the rifle ready. A cow moose followed by a calf stomped into the open and crossed my path without even a sidelong glance in my direction. It was quite a surprise to see them so far from more-typical moose habitat.

In a recent development, bob had good news back at the ranch that night. He had scouted in another direction and found many tracks.

In a recent development, “They seem to be paralleling Canyon Creek, heading down toward the old ghost camp,” Bob stated. “If the snow’s thinner, we might find them there tomorrow.”.

Recent findings suggest that the next morning was bitterly cold. We gathered in the ranch kitchen and huddled around the cook stove while George carved thick strips of bacon from a slab and mixed up a large bowl of sourdough pancake batter. It is a standard practical joke around Canyon Creek to conceal a round sheet of cardboard inside some unsuspecting diner’s pancake and then watch him try to cut it with a fork. George pulled the trick on John, and we had a good laugh before beginning a cold day.

It was possible to drive our four-wheel-drive rig partway to where Bob had found sign the day before. We parked our vehicle beside a small tributary of Canyon Creek, now almost completely frozen, and followed it on foot to an open meadow bordered by a wooded slope. There we found Bob’s tracks as well as deer tracks that had been made since his reconnaissance. It was soon evident that a herd of deer had fed along the meadow’s edges; in windswept places they had pawed circular areas free of snow to get at the vegetation underneath. But apparently the deer hadn’t lingered long, and their tracks disappeared in many different directions.

“Our best bet,” George said, “is to go separate ways and see what we find.”.

Because George knew the country best, he took a more complicated route, which led through heavy cover, wound around a mountainside, and nearly dead-ended at a steep rocky cliff. He figured that game might be bedded on top or near the face of the cliff.

Recent findings suggest that john and I proceeded together until the meandering tracks appeared to divide into two small herds. Then we separated, planning to meet late in the day on an unimproved road far below.

One set of the tracks I followed was very large, and I concentrated on it. I walked parallel to the buck’s path on the downwind side while watching far ahead for a glimpse of the animal. That technique had worked well for me on other hunts, and it might work again.

Recent findings suggest that I was so intent on following the buck that I almost stumbled over a bedded doe. She went flying in a cloud of snow down the slope. Then, before my hands were steady again, a shot cracked in the distance. The shot spooked a second deer about 150 yards to my right. I saw the animal for only an instant and couldn’t tell whether it was my buck. But when I hurried back to the buck’s trail, I found the spot where he had suddenly shifted into high gear.

In a recent development, for the rest of the day I stillhunted slowly but got no action. I was optimistic, however, for at last we were in deer country.

In a recent development, the shot I’d heard was George’s. He had broken the ice. About a mile from where he’d left John and me, he’d noticed that the tracks of the largest deer became more meandering — often an indication that a deer is seeking a good place to bed. George slowed his own pace accordingly, stopping often to scan thoroughly every bit of mountain terrain in front of him. This is the simplest and oldest of all mule-deer-hunting strategies, and once again it paid off.

Industry observers note that just before George reached a small draw, he stopped. Soon he saw a shape that put him on alert. On the slope slightly above him was the outline of a buck’s rack, somewhat obscured by a screen of brush. In the next moment the deer was on its feet and running. But it was slowed by snow, and it hadn’t gone more than 20 feet when George drilled a shot through the lungs. He found the animal dead 50 yards from where it had been hit.

The buck was an old, heavy five-pointer (Western count) with unusually heavy beams. It was a trophy that even an old-timer in the Montana Rockies could brag about. The buck, even when field-dressed, was a terrible weight to drag to the nearest pickup point. Without the slippery snow and all-downhill going, we would have needed a packhorse or two for the job.

It has been revealed that but the day produced more than a trophy mule deer for George. It also revealed that deer were moving from the high country into lower ranges where food was more available. The farther we had hunted that day, the more fresh tracks we had encountered. John reported jumping 12 deer from a sheltered meadow that, from the amount of tracks and digging in the snow, resembled a livestock pasture. None of the deer had the kind of rack that John was looking for, but his gloom early in the trip had been replaced by enthusiasm.

“Tomorrow,” he predicted to me, “both of us will score.”.

In a recent development, the next morning was overcast, and flurries of snow drifted to the ground as we huddled again around the kitchen stove. After breakfast George drove us to a spot close to where John had seen deer the day before. We had driven along that same trail several times before. Only two days before, John noted, the only track on the new snow had been made by a wandering coyote. Now deer tracks were everywhere.

George left John and me where the road forked. He would pick us up late in the afternoon at a point about two miles farther on.

Sources indicate that few thrills can match walking through woodlands that you know contain game. You are tense and excited, and it’s difficult to slow down and hunt carefully enough.

According to recent reports, john and I had scarcely separated when I saw deer running over an open ridge ahead and above me. I didn’t spot any antlers, but no matter. All the animals were out of range and gone before I would have had a shot.

“Slow down,” I noted to myself half-aloud. But my pulse was racing.

Industry observers note that that day I saw as many muleys as I’ve ever seen on a day’s hunt afoot. We had found a winter deer yard, and collecting venison would have been incredibly easy. But I kept hoping for the substantial buck. Actually I did see two together, but they were traveling and already 400 to 500 yards away.

At dusk when I came out again on the road, weary to the bone, I still hadn’t fired a shot. The headlights of George’s vehicle were a welcome sight in the gloom. Even better was the big buck lashed on top. John had scored, and back at the ranch he told about it.

Recent findings suggest that early in the morning, after his eagerness had spooked a very good buck, John decided to hunt more from the seat of his pants and less by hiking all over the landscape. When he found a good sheltered place, he sat down on a deadfall. Though the mountain slope opposite him seemed empty of game, he studied it through his glasses. Soon he focused on a spike buck, bedded and almost hidden behind a juniper bush. John shifted his gaze slightly upward, and there he saw the kind of buck he wanted.

Sources indicate that the four-pointer was bedded in a cluster of trees and was in deep shadow. But his antlers, outlined against the snow, gave him away. John figured that the range was more than 500 yards — much too far to risk a shot — but that by making good use of the cover on his side of the mountain he could cut the distance in half. He made the stalk successfully, and one shot from his Model 700 Remington .30/06 anchored the buck.

That left one day — the last day of the open season — for me to score.

Perhaps because of the intense cold in the bunkhouse the next morning, the alarm clock didn’t work and George had to awaken me.

“Look out the window,” he called, “and over toward Canyon Creek.”.

According to recent reports, there, in the crown of a dead spruce splintered long ago by lightning, sat the great gray owl. Probably another storm was on its way. As a result I wolfed my breakfast and, though I should have known better, got hooked on one of George’s cardboard pancakes.

Industry observers note that george drove me close to the deer yard we had found, and from there I started out on foot. It was not a pleasant morning to be afield. Scattered snow flurries were being driven by a wild bitter wind, which was promptly obliterating deer tracks and which made cautious hunting — stopping often to scan the slopes — very difficult. I had to keep moving to keep warm. By mid-morning I had found very few fresh tracks and had seen no deer. I figured that all or at least most of the deer had already moved to even lower elevations ahead of the new storm. My chances looked very poor.

Industry observers note that at noon I found some deadfalls on the edge of a dense spruce thicket that furnished a fairly good windbreak, and I sat down to munch a sandwich and a candy bar. The place also gave me a good view, between snow squalls, of distant, partly timbered mountainsides. Through binoculars I examined the wooded slopes, concentrating on those farthest away. As I glassed, I caught a slight movement much closer. Refocusing the glasses, I saw a forkhorn traveling slowly down the hill below me. He was less than 200 yards away, and though the crosswind wasn’t the best for shooting, it would not give me away.

Sources indicate that I decided I would have to take the forkhorn or get nothing at all. Slowly I raised my rifle and found a rest for it on the deadfall. The shot would have been easy, but as I was about to squeeze off, a second forkhorn strolled out into the open. Then, right behind him, came a third buck.

Industry observers note that at first I could see only the body of the third buck in my scope. But that was enough to tell me he was significant. As I watched, the buck changed direction and was hidden from view again. Should I take a chance and play the waiting game, or shoot one of the forkhorns, still in sight?

Recent findings suggest that the significant buck resolved my indecision when he appeared again. This time I could see his splendid rack. My 7 mm. was sighted-in for 200 yards, so I held the crosshairs on the point of the shoulder, adjusted for windage, and squeezed. The deer lurched forward, out of view; I didn’t know whether I’d connected.

I hurried down the steep slope and waded through a deep drift in a gully. I found the buck lying dead against a tree trunk. He was a fine four-pointer and as heavy a mule deer as I’ve ever bagged.

According to recent reports, that evening the great gray owl proved to be an accurate prophet. Another storm pounded the Rockies and plastered the high country with another layer of snow. But back at the ranch, I barely noticed it.

“The idea of the late hunt,” John said, “was sure a great one.”.

A Montana nonresident big-game license costs $151. A deer-only license, which entitles the holder to one deer in a specified district, is $35, plus $1 for a conservation license. This year the general season on deer in Montana runs from October 22 to November 26. But prospective hunters should write the Montana Fish and Game Department, Helena, Montana 59601, for a copy of the detailed hunting regulations.

Read Next: I Promised to Take My Boys Rabbit Hunting Every Day of Christmas Break.

The tag end of the season can be a good time for any big-game hunt. Almost everywhere in the West, the odds for connecting with a trophy head may be improved then, simply because the animals are not so high and are easier to find. Of course, there are unseasonably warm years when animals are not driven downward by deep snow until after the season ends. Remember too that late-season hunting can be very rugged — and occasionally impossible. It’s wise to know bad-weather and snow-survival techniques. But these are the chances a sportsman must take. And for my money, the rewards are worth the gamble.

Photographer Deidre Denali Rosenberg feels most at home in the high alpine, among deep talus fields, mountain meadows, and the places where treeline transitions to rock and scrub.

Coincidentally, talus and mountain meadows are also prime real estate for one very cute, sometimes loud, and occasionally plump high-alpine mammal: the American pika.

It has been revealed that rosenberg knows all about the American pika, which is the alpinist cousin of the rabbit; she’s been pointing her camera at them for over a decade, often spending enough time in certain areas that she’s gotten to know individual pikas over the years. In 2020, after many seasons traipsing through the mountains of the Four Corners region looking for and at pikas, Rosenberg began to notice more—we’ll say sturdy—pikas in the wild. And thus, an idea was born: Fat Pika Week.

Hunting Unpressured Bucks on One of the Best Properties in the Country

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we are well into deer season now, and bucks are definitely feeling the pressure. If you’re like the rest of us, you’re probably seeing daylight movement start to decrease on your trail cameras, or maybe it’s already dropped off. I’m right there with you. The places that I hunt see plenty of pressure, even though they’re on private ground. This week on the podcast, I’m talking to our gear editor, Scott Einsmann, who just came back from an incredibly unique experience: He was hunting almost completely unpressured mature bucks in the Midwest. Scott shares what that experience was like, what he learned from it, and how it can help him — and you — back in the real world of deer hunting. —Alex Robinson, editor-in-chief.

Listen to this episode on Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Alex Robinson: Hey, Scott, thanks for joining the Outdoor Life Podcast. I want to talk to you about your favorite thing in the world, which is bowhunting for whitetail deer.

According to recent reports, scott Einsmann: Awesome. Let’s do it. I just came off the most amazing week of bowhunting for whitetails.

Alex: Yeah. We’re coming up on the holiday season, and you have a good redemption story, and everybody loves a good redemption story around the holidays. So to start this off, explain the property that you’re able to hunt in Illinois. What’s it like, and how did you weasel your way into getting bowhunting access to this place?

According to recent reports, scott: It’s 800 acres in southern Illinois, and what makes it a really good 800 acres is, one, it has topography, and it also has large wood blocks in it, and it’s surrounded by significant ag fields. So once all the crops are cut, all the deer get sucked right into this property. For that reason, it’s just insane hunting. There are really good deer. There’s not a 200-incher on it, but there are a ton of 130- to 150-inch deer, and a ton of really good 8-points — some really cool deer. Last year, some big 6-points were killed, which is always fun. And maybe 300 does just running around this place. I mean, it’s crazy.

Alex: So talk about whose property it is and how you’re able to get on it, because you’re not a multimillionaire property owner.

Alex: A lot of these properties are either owned or leased by — you know, it’s the stuff that everybody dreams about hunting, but not everybody really gets access to.

According to recent reports, scott: Yes. And I did inquire with the farm manager there: How does someone get a lease in this area? You really just have to know the local farmers, because a lot of them have been burned by people leasing their property and not treating it right. So you really have to have someone to vouch for you and then be part of the community.

Luckily, I know someone. Levi Morgan and Andy Morgan have the lease for this property, and they have several leases in the area now, and they’re all pretty incredible. But this one they’ve had the longest — about three years now — and they’re really starting to dial it in and understand how the deer use it. They’re connected with our friends at Tactacam Reveal, and part of being an outdoor writer is you get to go on press trips.

Sources indicate that press trips vary in quality and fun. But this one is by far the best I’ve ever been on, because it’s not a guided hunt. You’re not just being driven around by an outfitter and sitting over a corn pile somewhere. We go out there in the summer, we hang stands, we hang cameras, get to learn the property a little bit, and then we have access to those cameras all season long — which for me is great, because my home lease is not that exciting by comparison.

In a recent development, scott: So just being able to scroll and see cool deer after cool deer — and they have a ton of turkeys as well, and I have some good news there. So we have access to all that, and then we come back in November and hunt the place during the peak of the rut.

And it is so much fun to be in a place where you get to see whitetail deer acting like whitetail deer, because it gets hunted two weeks out of the year, by bowhunters only. There’s no gun hunting on it. So it’s a substantial property with very limited pressure, and these deer act like deer. They’re out in the middle of the day. There’s this one field right by the hog barn, and there’s a little strip of beans in it, but the rest is wheat or rye or something like that. It’s a huge field. At 1 o’clock in the afternoon on any given day, there’s a dozen does out there, and there’s probably going to be a buck checking every one of those does. It’s a really hard place to kill a deer, but it’s a fun place to watch deer.

It’s just an example. There are just deer out like that. In my area, in the Southeast, you would never see that, because someone’s going to take a shot at those deer from the road.

Recent findings suggest that alex: Yeah, I mean, even my area of Wisconsin and Minnesota — you’ve got a couple people hunting every, say, 80 acres, right? If you split up all the farmland around my area of western Wisconsin, there’s probably one hunter per 80 acres hunting pretty much every weekend. Some of those guys are very good hunters and they’re holding out for significant bucks. Other folks are just out there for fun and they’re going to shoot whatever. There’s a lot in between, but there is hunting pressure basically from October through the heart of the gun season, which we’re in right now.

Recent findings suggest that we have private property in north-central Wisconsin that my family always hunts, and opening day of gun season, it’s like a war zone. You just hear gunfire from all directions echoing through the morning, basically that entire first day. You can see the neighbors on their properties. Some folks will sit right on the property line. And even though we’re hunting private land, the deer know that they’re being hunted, and it’s a high-pressure situation. And that’s not even considering public land, right? So you have this view into a world that very few —.

Alex: Very few places even exist like this, where deer can just be deer throughout basically the fall cycle.

Scott: Yeah, pretty much. And I’m lucky to be at a place in my hunting career where I really, really appreciate it. I know how good it is and how lucky I am.

Alex: So this is your second crack at it this season. And not to dredge up the dark times, but I feel like enough time has passed now: You hunted out there last season. Talk about what went down.

Industry observers note that scott: So last season, one, we didn’t hit the chase period — the rut — as well as we did this year. So we weren’t really seeing a ton of deer, by the standards of this place in Illinois.

According to recent reports, scott: This was maybe day three or so. I had sat a stand on this cool little food plot that we have down there, and some guy just ends up walking in on the setup around 8 or 9 o’clock in the morning.

Alex: Like, trespassing into it?

Sources indicate that scott: Yes, trespassing into it. I took a picture of him real quick and shot a text to Levi and Andy, who had already killed their deer, so they were just helping everybody else kill. They said they would be there lickety-split. We said hi to the guy, and he looked up like a doe who just realized that you were there. Just busted. And he said, “Oh, sorry,” and then he left. I was like, “That was so weird. I don’t know who that was or what they were doing here.”.

And it turns out that in Andy and Levi’s truck was the farm manager, John, who is a character all of his own. We should do a documentary about him. He’s such an interesting individual. So they’re pulling in, and they see this guy leaving where we’re at. Before the truck even stops, John is out of the truck running up to this guy, and he just unloads a verbal assault on him. Andy and Levi are in the truck in shock, like, “Oh my God, is there about to be a huge fight?” But this guy understood that he was in the wrong, and he backed off, apologized and left. Turns out he was living next door, and they believe he was being evicted, and they think he was coming to look for something to steal before he left.

Sources indicate that scott: Yeah. Luckily that didn’t happen.

Alex: So, like, maybe trying to grab some trail cameras or —.

Scott: Yeah, trail cameras or something, whatever. Not the most upstanding citizen of McLeansboro, Illinois.

It has been revealed that alex: OK. All right. So we’ve got this going on in the middle of your hunt.

Scott: Yeah. So that spot is blown, but I’m watching trail camera feeds nonstop. And that morning, there was a good deer in this food plot just up the hill from where we were sitting, and we had seen him from that spot. They were like, “He might come back there this evening. Let’s try to get into that stand.” So we get up there. It’s called Liquid Death, and it’s right next to a plot called Andy’s Plot. So you have these two food plots that are right next to each other, and right behind the stand you have a really nice watering hole.

In a recent development, we see some does throughout the day into the evening, and then it’s the last hour of daylight and we see a buck way off. There are some does right up on the hill that this food plot leads up to, and he bumps one of those does down. She comes down into the food plot pretty close to us, like 30-ish yards. And then he’s up there on this hill, sun going down, perfect golden-hour lighting, just looking unbelievably majestic. Oh, and by the way, I have a camera guy over my shoulder filming all this.

According to recent reports, so then he follows that doe right down into the plot. I had ranged little empty spots in the food plot, or little shadows, earlier in the day, but now it’s last light. There are no shadows.

Industry observers note that scott: But also my brain was not working. I don’t know exactly what my thought process was, but I was at full draw, and I dropped my 35 pin behind the shoulder and shot. As soon as the arrow hit, it was like, ugh, because it did not penetrate even a little bit. You could just see it hanging out. And he bounds off and stands at 60 yards.

Recent findings suggest that scott: Yeah, a high shoulder hit. And he’s standing there right at 60, looking around, not sure what just happened. He stood there for a while, and then he just walks off into the woods. And I was just like, “What just happened?” I think everyone knows that thick feeling when you know you just screwed up substantial time — especially because it was a great deer, a really nice, tall 8-point.

It has been revealed that so what had happened is I shot him for 35, and he was 30. And looking back at the slow-motion footage, he dropped a few inches. Also, his leg that was closest to me was back, and that arrow hit the upper portion of the scapula — there’s that hard ridge right there. The arrow hit that bone square. So it didn’t even hit the soft part of the scapula, where you might have a chance. It hit right on that bone. I would imagine that deer survived. We looked all the next day, and we didn’t find anything but a few drops of blood.

Industry observers note that alex: Yeah, that’s a nonlethal hit with archery equipment pretty much every time. You’re just kind of screwed. That’s not where you want to shoot a deer, you know?

Scott: No. If you’re trying to kill one, that’s not the spot to hit them.

Scott: And to make matters worse, I’ve been a fan of archery my whole life, and Levi Morgan is the guy in 3D archery — definitely the greatest of the current generation, and in the conversation for greatest 3D archer of all time. And he’s across the field watching this with some other guys, and their binoculars all go down. Oh, no. So someone you look up to is watching you screw up. Even worse.

In a recent development, alex: Yeah. And he has you on his property to hunt these massive deer. And you’re like, “I’m an Outdoor Life archery guy. I can do this. I’ve bowhunted my entire life. This is my thing.”.

Industry observers note that scott: Yeah. And there were a lot of things I did wrong there, obviously. I think the moment was so substantial — this really cool sequence of events — and I just didn’t take the second to range. My rangefinder was right there. I could’ve just clicked and confirmed, but in the moment I was like, “Yep, that’s 35, maybe.” That little short circuit is ultimately what it was, because the shot-execution part was fine.

Industry observers note that alex: It’s not like you hit far back. You basically hit where you were aiming, right? You were just aiming with the wrong pin, or you were not holding low enough.

Sources indicate that scott: Yeah. It’s the dumbest of all mistakes to make.

Sources indicate that alex: Going back to the unpressured deer, one thing that I have noticed — especially with more mature bucks in the rut — is you can get away with so much more than we often think. Especially if you’re used to hunting deer earlier in the year, or shooting does, where any little movement or any little mistake and their attention is on you. There have been times where I’ve tried to stop a buck with the classic “meh” to get them to stop walking so I can shoot, and they’re 20 yards away and they don’t stop. I’ve had to yell to get their attention, because they’re just in that rut mode.

And I guess my point is I’ve made mistakes of being in the tree and thinking, “OK, I can’t range. I need to just shoot, because if I try to range and then draw, he’s going to see me draw, and I just have to make this shot.” Oftentimes you can range. Even if the buck’s in the open, you can draw, and maybe they see you and stop and then you can shoot them, or maybe they don’t even see you.

It has been revealed that scott: Yeah. And it was also an open field, so it’s not like you could range some trees and have real landmarks — which I guess I’m not very used to. I don’t hunt a lot of open fields. But talking to Levi this year about what he does in the tree when a buck is coming in, he has his rangefinder in his hand and is ranging the deer as it’s coming in, thinking about all the possible places where that buck could end up in front of him. He’s one of the best people in the world at judging distance, and he’s still ranging the deer as it comes in until he gets a shot.

Recent findings suggest that alex: Yeah. A world-champion 3D archer is doing this.

It has been revealed that scott: Yes. And he said he wants to know the exact distance that deer is at before he pulls back his bow.

Sources indicate that alex: On my tree harness, I have a little clip that I clip my rangefinder to, so I can range and then just drop it, and it stays on my harness. I don’t have to shove it back in my pocket or take it out. Honestly, I started doing that after a similar situation to yours. I shot a buck that was closer than I thought, and because of that, I didn’t hit him well and didn’t get him. And I was like, “OK, now I need to range every shot, unless it’s obviously 20 yards or closer.”.

Sources indicate that scott: Yeah. And I’ve also started aiming a little lower. I was aiming mid-body behind the shoulder, but now I’m aiming at the top of the heart, especially on those closer shots.

Alex: OK. So let’s move to this year. What was your hunt like this year? How’d that play out?

Scott: So this year, we hit a cold front just as we were arriving. It was pretty incredible, actually, to have that timing — perfect weather, ideal conditions. The deer were chasing. You could see it all on the trail cameras from 10 a.m. until 3 p.m. Bucks everywhere.

In a recent development, scott: The day that we arrived, we were planning on trying to get out in the stand. We all got there around noon, but we were like, “We can’t, because there are deer everywhere and we’ll just end up bumping them. It’s better to sneak in in the morning and then hunt.” And so that’s what we did.

Sources indicate that one really cool thing that I’ve learned from Levi and Andy is how to hunt deer without them knowing that they’re being hunted. They are very particular about their entry and exit routes into the stands — getting in clean, getting out clean, in terms of wind direction, ground scent and just not bumping deer on your way to a stand location. So they have some really cool, sneaky spots where you can very easily get in and get out.

It has been revealed that the one I was hunting, there are these train tracks that run through a portion of the property, and they have three stands right off the train tracks. You drive a side-by-side down the train tracks, go maybe 50 yards into the woods, and you’re up a tree. So it’s real easy, with no chance of really bumping anything, and you just sit there all day. For the most part, they’re on pinch points between food and bedding, or on natural travel corridors. I mean, there isn’t a bad spot on this property, but these ones in particular are very, very cool.

Alex: I have a quick question on that. You have all this camera activity and you’re getting pictures of all these bucks, and obviously some places are going to be a little harder to access than others. And then you have these train-track stands that are super sneaky to get in and out of. I feel like I know the answer to this, but if there’s one camera that has a giant buck on it, but there’s a probability of spooking deer on that access, versus these other cameras where you know you can get in clean and out clean — which one are they going to send you to?

Scott: The ones you can get in and out clean.

Alex: Even though you only have a few days to hunt, they’re like, “No matter what, we’re not going to spook deer.”.

Scott: Pretty much. For example, that stand I hunted last year — this year, Levi shot a really nice buck out of that same stand. And right after that, there were more massive bucks on that same food plot every single day. But nobody hunted it, because you can’t get in there in the morning without bumping them. It’s a food plot, and the only access is to walk down the edge of the woods. The other problem is the wind direction ended up switching. So you’d have to try to get in there in the middle of the day, but the deer were so active in the middle of the day that that whole really awesome spot with good deer on it didn’t end up being huntable.

Another part of this approach is they’re really hunting the outer perimeter of the property and not going right into the middle. Last year we had trail cameras down in these creek bottoms, and it was like a deer highway, especially in the middle of the day — big bucks just cruising up and down. But we didn’t hunt them, because there’s too great a chance of getting busted in there. When the thermals switch, the wind has to be so perfect that it’s not worth the risk of going right into the middle of the property and trying to kill a deer, because you’re going to blow the whole property out on that one attempt. Maybe if it was just your property you could do whatever you want, but there are other people trying to kill bucks at the same time.

Industry observers note that alex: So the reason the deer are the way they are is, one, because it’s only hunted two weeks out of the year. But two, the way that it’s hunted, the deer don’t even feel the pressure that they have on them, because they’re just not bumping into humans or human scent.

Sources indicate that scott: Right. And in the places where they are — I mean, it’s an active farm. They’re used to seeing people on the farm roads and stuff.

Alex: OK. I’m starting to get it.

Scott: And just to hit that point a little bit more: When you do bump a deer going in, if you’re accessing through an area where they’re used to seeing people, those deer will be right back.

In a recent development, alex: Yeah. It’s not like you’re bumping them out of their bedding area or their main feeding area. Got it. All right, go on with your hunt for this year.

Recent findings suggest that scott: So back to the redemption day. I’m in this stand. Another thing about hunting with Levi and Andy is they like to hang their stands very high. One of the guys got into one and ranged it, and it was 12 or 13 yards to the bottom of the tree. So like 36 feet in the air. They’re not all that high, but they’re all at least 20 feet up.

Sources indicate that alex: Why do they do that? For scent, or so you don’t get seen, or they just like it?

Recent findings suggest that scott: A little bit of both. I talked to Levi about this last year. It’s just how he grew up hunting. His dad always hung the stands really high, because he’s from North Carolina, where deer actually do look up into trees as they walk. So this is what he’s used to and what he’s always done. And Levi’s also really tall. He’s 6-foot-4. So if you’re shorter than 6-foot-4, you might have to make some jumps as you climb up the sticks, because of the gap between the sticks. Luckily I didn’t have that problem.

Alex: OK. So somehow you made it way high up there.

Industry observers note that scott: I’m high up in the tree. I’ve got a camera guy with me, and the stand looks higher than it is because it’s up on a hill, and you’re looking down at a couple trails that are at the bottom of this hill. So it’s a pretty steep downward angle.

The morning was pretty quiet for the most part. That first hour of daylight, I saw some deer, nothing crazy. Saw a coyote. Heard the most amazing turkey vocalizations of all time — a huge group of hens behind us, everything in the book. It was nuts, and loud. So that was cool for me. And then we had an 8-point come in at about 15 yards — a really nice, maybe 3-year-old typical 8-point. But the camera guy couldn’t get on him. And I mean, it’s the first morning.

3 Totally Normal Deer Hunting Tactics We Used to Think Were Utter Nonsense

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When they were first introduced to the national hunting community, these novel methods for bringing in bucks were considered unconventional at best, and harebrained schemes by most.
  • The brush-country hunters of Texas and Fresh Mexico were crashing antlers together for decades before the trend caught fire in the rest of whitetail country.
  • “He was coming to town one day, his wagon loaded with deer carcasses, when a buck came barging out of the mesquite,” reads one May 1951 story from OL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When they were first introduced to the national hunting community, these novel methods for bringing in bucks were considered unconventional at best, and harebrained schemes by most. Now deer hunters everywhere use these tried-and-true tactics. We take a look back to when these trusty standbys were still considered downright bizarre.

The brush-country hunters of Texas and Fresh Mexico were crashing antlers together for decades before the trend caught fire in the rest of whitetail country. Although Native hunters almost certainly developed the technique, legend has it that an old market hunter accidentally discovered the phenomenon.

“He was coming to town one day, his wagon loaded with deer carcasses, when a buck came barging out of the mesquite,” reads one May 1951 story from OL. “The hunter, so the story goes, added him to the load. A short time later, another buck pranced up — and was soon in the wagon. The puzzled hunter stopped to figure things out and discovered that two carcasses were lying so their antlers clashed as the wagon jounced along the rough country road.”.

Related: How to Rattle in a Buck, Based on Whitetail Deer Research.

Our first story devoted to rattling appeared in October 1937. A Texas game warden, drawing on 30 years of experience with the tactic, taught author Fredric P. Schwab exactly how to sound like “two bucks in a life-and-death struggle.”.

By the 1950s, most hunters in the rest of the country had heard of rattling, but few had tried it. Almost everyone who had tried tickling tines reported the method didn’t work on hill-country deer, although a rare hunter outside the Lone-Star State would claim success. Here’s what modern research indicates about the efficacy of rattling in deer.

The concept of calling for deer was less established even than rattling in the middle of the 20th century. In August 1949, an experienced deer hunter traveled to Alaska for a Sitka blacktail hunt. “He was sure it was just a gag,” reads the story. “Who ever head of calling a buck?”.

“Now I’ve used crow calls, duck calls, and turkey calls, and I’d read that down in Texas they lure bucks by rattling a couple of antlers together. But a real deer call I’d never heard of. Probably my voice expressed my skepticism. ‘O.K. I’ll bite. What’s a deer call?’”.

Read Now: When and How to Use a Grunt Tube to Call in Deer.

Industry observers note that the Alaskan hunters employed the call often — which looks a bit like a harmonica and sounds like “a lost lamb bleating for its mother,” — but they admit they don’t know what sound it was supposed to replicate. “I’ve attracted does as well as bucks, so I don’t think it’s a mating call,” said one local. “An old Indian told me it’s the cry of a fawn in mortal terror,” said another.

In the end, the author and a fellow hunter call in two bucks and drop both of them. This story, “A Deer Call Brings ‘Em In!” garnered so much reader mail that an advice column on using commercial calls appeared in the August 1949 matter. The expert claimed to have used his call with excellent results on 100 wild deer, and that his call was a modern counterpart of those made by Native Americans in Alaska. So while calls were being produced commercially by the late 40s, they remained news to most hunters.

Although a variety of products designed to lure bucks and cover up human odor had been marketed for years, it appears most hunters initially considered the scents for sale at the local sporting goods shop akin to something hawked by a snake oil salesman.

Read Next: 15 Scent Control Strategies That Actually Work for Deer Hunting.

“It was probably because I was growing desperate that I decided to buy the deer scent,” writes John Weiss, author of the November 1978 feature “Scents and Nonscents.” “I figured there was nothing to lose.”.

Weiss reported that more than 50 companies made scents at the time, and were raking in an estimated $37 million a year. That included everything from hunter’s soaps and food attractants to tarsal scents and urine.

He then delved into the types of scents and their effectiveness, and dug into the “scientific” realm of deer hunting. Interestingly, most biologists interviewed for the story disregarded “a deer’s scenting ability as not all that key.” One researcher noted that a deer’s “visual capabilities are far more refined than hearing or smelling abilities.”.

Yet most wildlife biologists today agree that a deer’s nose is it’s most formidable asset. Nonscents, indeed. It makes you wonder: If these are the facts we believed back then, just think about what we’ve got wrong now. And, even more fun to imagine, is what idiotic tactic might be all the rage in another couple decades.

This story, “‘Wacky’ Deer Tactics,” first appeared in the Oct. 2015 matter of Outdoor Life.

7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • Sources indicate that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • In a recent development, being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no prepares for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Sources indicate that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

In a recent development, being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no prepares for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

Industry observers note that after landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

Sources indicate that however, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

It has been revealed that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden said, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

Industry observers note that linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival rapidly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

One of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling strategy was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden remarked. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

In a recent development, assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other prepares. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

It has been revealed that next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden stated. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden stated, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

When things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden stated. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

Sources indicate that while Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden said. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

Outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

And they do. There’s no one else here. By some estimates, Spain has more than three thousand abandoned villages. I was in one called Las Casillas de Bezas, in the eastern half of the country, in the province of Teruel, high-stepping over brambles, ducking as swallows darted around my head, and wondering if I was striding into the ancient past or the deep future.

Winter Bivy Sack Guide (2026)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sectionhiker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that winter bivy sacks are different from three-season bivy sacks, which are often used in conjunction with a tarp for insect and splashback protection, where rain hitting the ground can bounce back and wet your quilt or sleeping bag.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that winter bivy sacks were first developed as solo shelters for mountaineering and climbing where participants were interested in lightweight and highly compressible camping gear. Bivy Sacks are also an attractive option for backpacking hunters, backcountry skiers, and winter backpackers who want the lightest and smallest shelter they can carry for overnight or emergency use.

Sources indicate that winter bivy sacks are different from three-season bivy sacks, which are often used in conjunction with a tarp for insect and splashback protection, where rain hitting the ground can bounce back and wet your quilt or sleeping bag. In contrast, a winter bivy sack is intended as a standalone shelter or used with a snow shelter such as a trench or snow cave. Winter bivy sacks tend to be much higher in volume to hold winter-weight sleeping bags without compressing the insulation and work best in dry and cold conditions where precipitation is in the form of snow.

The biggest advantage of a winter bivy sack is that you can use it anywhere you want to stop and sleep. Most models don’t require tent stakes or poles, and they pack down very small, which is great when you want to keep your winter gear lightweight and compact. Most winter bivy sacks use waterproof/breathable top fabrics to reduce internal condensation and waterproof base fabrics to keep your sleeping bag and pad dry. Insect netting is also available in some cold weather bivy sacks and can be useful when they’re used in spring conditions when bugs begin to emerge,.

There are many advantages to sleeping in a waterproof bivy sack over a tent. It is easy to find a place to put a bivy sack at night since it only requires as much space as your sleeping pad and sleeping bag. Simply unroll your bivy sack, slip your sleeping pad and sleeping bag inside, and crawl in. This makes them suitable for sleeping on narrow mountain ledges or in forested glades where there’s just enough space to lie between two trees.

In a recent development, there are no tent stakes to freeze into the ground so you can get inside without delay and get warm. Being waterproof, you don’t have to lie on top of a groundsheet either, since the bottom of a waterproof bivy sack is designed to keep you dry. Bivy sacks also add a few degrees of insulation to your sleep system and make great emergency shelters for solo winter hikers, provided you carry a sleeping pad and enough insulation to get through the night.

Bivy sacks are much more confining than tents, with only enough space for you and a few small personal items. You can’t really do anything inside one except listen to podcasts or go to sleep. It’s awkward to change out of your wet clothes or put on dry clothes inside, depending on the type of bivy sack you have; it can be damn hard to put on your boots, even to go for a pee at night. There’s no place to store your backpack, and the rest of your gear will be fully exposed at night without any cover.

Recent findings suggest that bivy sacks are also more prone to internal condensation than a tent, even when manufactured with waterproof breathable materials. You’re best off keeping them open or unzipped at night to reduce the temperature difference between the inside of the bivy and the outside, which causes condensation. Tent condensation occurs for the same reason, but tents have better ventilation and more volume, so it’s easier to keep your sleeping bag dry when it occurs.

In a recent development, despite these disadvantages, I have friends who swear by their winter bivy sacks because they’re so fast to deploy compared to a tent or tarp. I’ve used winter bivy sacks and can appreciate their strengths, but winter nights last a very long time, and it’s nice to have a little extra space to change your clothes or sleep with your gear inside your tent. Whichever you choose depends on what you’re trying to accomplish.

There are three types of winter bivy sacks to choose from:.

In a recent development, there are two types of hooped bivy sacks: those with front entrances that you slide into feet first and those that you can enter from the side. Both come with one more short fiberglass or carbon fiber rods that give shape to the hood and prevent it from collapsing onto your head or torso.

Recent findings suggest that the head-end of a hooped front entrance bivy is usually screened with a solid cover that can be zippered closed for warmth or to block wind or rain. This design provides good ventilation for your head and helps to expel the water vapor in your breath. The Outdoor Research Helium UL Bivy is a good example of the front entry hooped design.

Sources indicate that side-entry hooped bivy sacks usually have a zipper along one side so you can easily get in and out of them. This design is also easier to vent because you can roll up the top cover in dry weather to reduce internal condensation. The Outdoor Research Alpine XT Bivy is a good example of a hooped bivy with a side entrance.

The simplest and lightest-weight winter bivy sacks are little more than sleeping bag covers. Some have drawstrings that you can pull closed over your head; some have shaped mummy-style hoods or simple slits above the face for ventilation. While not as livable or as well-ventilated as the hooped bivy sack designs described above, they do the job if you want a highly compressible, ultralight weather protection for your sleep system.

There are multiple features and trade-offs to consider when choosing a winter bivy sack.

Industry observers note that A waterproof/breathable top fabric is vital for venting water vapor and reducing internal condensation that can make your sleeping bag wet. However, unlike rain jackets, most bivy sack manufacturers do not list the laboratory measurements used to rate waterproofing (hydrostatic head, abbreviated “HH”) or breathability (movable water transmission rate, abbreviated “MVTR”). That can make performance comparisons between different bivy sacks difficult.

Recent findings suggest that if headroom matters, consider a bivy shelter with a hooped design. These bivy sacks come with a flexible pole that slides into the hood to create more volume around your face and shoulders. The tradeoff is that they tend to be heavier than more minimal bivy sacks.

Winter bivy sacks tend to be high volume to fit bulky winter sleeping bags and inflatable pads with a high R-value. When choosing a bivy sack you want to ensure that there is enough room for your sleeping bag insulation to fully loft and that it’s not compressed by having too tight a fit.

It’s much easier to get in and out of a bivy sack that has a zipper along the side than one that only has a “hatch” at the head end, to crawl in and out of. You’ll stay drier if the ground is covered in snow and it’s much easier to put on and take off your shoes.

If you initiative to bivy in early spring when biting insects emerge, make sure to get a winter bivy sack with a mesh panel over the face so you can sleep without insects biting your face at night. If you only plan to sleep in a bivy sack in winter or in snow caves, a mesh panel will be less important. For warmer weather use, I’d encourage you to invest in an ultralight bivy sack or bug shelter rather than a winter bivy sack, since they’re much cooler to use. See our 10 Best Backpacking Bug Shelters for our recommended three-season bivy sacks.

Don’t forget to consider the weight of the bivy sack and its packed size, since one of the chief benefits of using a bivy sack is gear weight and size reduction. There’s often a tradeoff between features and weight/size, but some winter bivy sacks are surprisingly lightweight and compressible.

Sources indicate that when in doubt, order a bivy sack (check the retailer’s return policy) and lie in it at home to see if it fits. This will probably tell you a lot more about whether it will work for you than comparing the specs of multiple models listed online. Check that you can fit your sleeping pad and sleeping bag inside, and that the footbox is large enough for your feet.

There is a class of emergency bivy sacks that are only intended for emergency use such as the SOL Escape Lite Bivy. These are made with thin reflective aluminized fabric and lack the durability or breathability of the multiuse bivy sacks listed above.

Industry observers note that turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie, and football. In America, that’s usually what’s on the menu on the fourth Thursday in November. But in the fall of 1621, the original Thanksgiving meal didn’t resemble this in the slightest. The Pilgrims at Plymouth Plantation had a lot to be thankful for. The Wampanoag helped them survive the previous winter and harvest plenty of food over the summer. The two groups decided to come together and celebrate this for a few days with a feast, during which they ate a mix of wild fish and game. Here is an excerpt from one of two firsthand accounts from a man named Edward Winslow:.

“Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors. They four in one day killed as much fowl as, with a little help beside, served the organization almost a week. At which time, amongst other recreations, we exercised our arms, many of the Indians coming amongst us, and among the rest their greatest king Massasoit, with some ninety men, whom for three days we entertained and feasted, and they went out and killed five deer, which they brought to the plantation and bestowed on our governor, and upon the captain and others.”.

That sounds a little more like deer camp than grandma’s house. Along with a pile of venison and week’s supply of fowl, it’s not out of the question to assume there were also dried fruits, berries, nuts, fish, and shellfish at the feast. Being that most of these things are available to hunters and anglers, we took a deep dive into some of our favorite recipes. In the spirit of that original Thanksgiving meal, here are eight ways to bring back some wild game to the table this season.

Sources indicate that the Wampanoag demonstrated the colonists a lot ways to grow and keep food, but neither group had access to refrigeration. Instead, things like berries and other fruit had to be eaten fresh or preserved. The most likely way they would have done this is by drying, but there’s another way to preserve fruit without refrigeration. Canning has been done for generations, and it’s still a perfect way to preserve wild berries for months. The pilgrims wouldn’t have had the sugar for this wild black raspberry jam recipe, but it still goes good with butter and toast, on a leftover turkey sandwich, or even some acorn-flour pancakes.

Today lobsters and other shellfish are considered delicacies, but 400 years ago, they were a staple. The Atlantic coastline provided Wampanoag and the colonists with clams, mussels, and lobster. But there’s also another crustacean, readily available in freshwater, that’s just as worthy of dipping in clarified butter: the crayfish. Here’s a classic crayfish etouffee to serve alongside the main course.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, melt the butter and add the flour. You are going to make a roux: over medium heat, stir the roux until it darkens to the color of peanut butter (about 20 minutes). Add the onions, celery, and green peppers, stirring to combine. Add the garlic, tomato paste, and Worcestershire. Stir for a couple of minutes. Pour in the stock and the cooked crayfish tail meat. Stir for a few minutes until the roux in well incorporated into the stock and it starts to boil. Turn the heat down to a simmer, and add the Cajun seasoning. Then simmer for about 20 minutes until the etouffee thickens. Serve over wild rice or plain white rice. If you like yours a little hotter, add Crystal hot sauce or your favorite hot sauce.

In the first sentence of the Winslow account, there’s a mention of fowl:.

“Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors.”.

Turkey is considered fowl, but the first thanksgiving probably included waterfowl instead. Ducks and geese would have been easier for the settlers and the Wampanoag to catch and cook. They are also more plentiful in the wild. The birds were most likely roasted over a fire. Spit roasting a whole bird is an involved process, and most will opt for an oven instead, given a chance. If you’re thinking about swapping duck for a turkey this year, this wild duck and squash curry is an excellent place to start.

It has been revealed that another bird readily available in the 17th century was the passenger pigeon. When populations were at their peak, it is said that flocks were so thick they would black out the sky. Unfortunately, this didn’t last. Due to heavy market hunting and habitat loss, the passenger pigeon is now extinct. A similar bird (though not closely related) is the mourning dove. In fact, one of the last living wild passenger pigeons was found roosting with mourning doves.

In a recent development, A classic popper recipe will work with doves and most other upland birds (and it also pairs well with football). But most dove hunters already have that recipe figured out. Instead, here’s a flaky cheese and pepper dove roll recipe that’s sure to please.

According to recent reports, fish played a substantial part in the colonist’s lives. They were loaned money to start the colony, and they planned to pay some of their debts back by fishing. Atlantic white cod would have been the fish of choice, though they would have also had access to other fish like runs Atlantic salmon. Here’s a linguini with salmon cream sauce recipe that makes use of the leftover, extra meat after filleting a fish.

In a recent development, bring a large stock pot with salted water to a boil over high heat and cook your pasta according to the directions on the package. Reserve one cup of the pasta water before draining. Drain the noodles and set aside in a colander until ready to use.

According to recent reports, in a large pan, melt the butter over medium heat, add the shallots and garlic, and cook until soft (about 2 minutes). Season with a pinch of salt, and black pepper to taste. Add the wine and cook until almost all the wine is evaporated. Add the heavy cream and the parmesan and stir together, cooking until the cream thickens up a bit (1-2 minutes). Add the pasta and toss with the cream sauce. If the sauce is too thick, add some of the pasta water until you get a creamy sauce. Toss in the parsley, and serve topped with grated parmesan. This will make six healthy servings.

Industry observers note that deer meat was likely the centerpiece of the first thanksgiving. After all, the Wampanoag brought five deer with them to the feast. Simple but effective, here’s the best way to apply heat to a backstrap and achieve perfection. And, just in case you have five deer on hand and a village to feed, here’s a guide on how to cook every scrap of meat on them.

According to recent reports, so where did this turkey thing come from anyway? The one other written account from the autumn of 1621 does mention that the pilgrims had turkey, although nobody is certain that it was eaten at the feast. The second account from William Bradford states:.

“And besides waterfowl there was great store of wild turkeys, of which they took many, besides venison, etc.”.

In a recent development, long after Bradford’s death, his journal was found and reprinted in the 1850s, and for some reason, people really liked the part about turkey. During that time, Sarah Josepha Hale, the editor of a magazine called Godey’s Lady’s Book, promoted the turkey as a centerpiece of the table. Hale was also a strong voice behind Thanksgiving Day becoming a national holiday. She wrote letters and even petitioned a few presidents.

Finally, in 1863, Abraham Lincoln declared the day a national holiday, and turkey has been the star of the show ever since. Whether wild turkey was eaten during the first Thanksgiving or not, it’s still delicious. If you have a left-over gobbler from the spring, or one you’ve shot this fall, this wild take on a classic Thanksgiving turkey recipe is sure to get some attention at your table.

• 2 gallons water • 2 oranges • 2 lemons • 1 onion, cut into 8 pieces • 1 cup brown sugar • 1 cup Kosher salt • Couple sprigs of fresh thyme or rosemary.

Make brining mixture, mixing all ingredients. Squeeze the oranges and lemons into the mixture and toss in the rinds too. Soak turkey in a cooler with ice and the brining mixture overnight. If you need more brine, use ½ cup salt and ½ cup brown sugar for every gallon of water. Use additional fruit as desired.

I lightly stuff the turkey with a couple celery stalks, onion pieces and a couple carrots, along with a half lemon and half orange from the brine mixture.

Sources indicate that 1. Place the turkey breast side up on a rack in a shallow roasting pan. Do not add water.

Industry observers note that 2. Before placing the turkey in the oven, you may want to brush it with cooking oil, melted butter or margarine, although it’s not necessary.

Industry observers note that 3. Cover the turkey with a loose tent of heavy-duty aluminum foil to prevent over browning, allow for maximum heat circulation and keep the turkey moist. To make a tent, tear off a sheet of foil 5 to 10 inches longer than the turkey. Crease the foil crosswise through the center and place over the turkey, crimping loosely onto the sides of the pan to hold it in place.
