    #160717. The Story of the Mickey Buck, Michigan’s State-Record Nontypical Swamp Buck

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 25m • 📚 Deep Dive (4922 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

    The Story of the Mickey Buck, Michigan’s State-Record Nontypical Swamp Buck

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that this story, “Swamped by Trophy Bucks,” appeared in the December 1980 problem of Outdoor Life.
    • I’d bet 10 to 1 there are at least 20 whitetail bucks within a 50-mile radius of my home that have racks good enough to be listed in the Pope and Young or Boone and Crockett record books.
    • It has been revealed that there are millions of people in this area, but there are also farmlands and swamps that produce some of the nation’s finest trophy whitetails.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that this story, “Swamped by Trophy Bucks,” appeared in the December 1980 problem of Outdoor Life. Mickey’s buck, which scored 238 2/8 according to the Boone and Crockett Club record books, remains the largest nontypical ever killed by a hunter in Michigan. It’s ranked as the No. 2 buck in the state, however, after a 246 2/8 deadhead found by Ronald A. Waldron in 2010.

    I’d bet 10 to 1 there are at least 20 whitetail bucks within a 50-mile radius of my home that have racks good enough to be listed in the Pope and Young or Boone and Crockett record books. I live near Bay City, Michigan, not far from the other big cities of Flint and Saginaw and less than 100 miles from Detroit.

    It has been revealed that there are millions of people in this area, but there are also farmlands and swamps that produce some of the nation’s finest trophy whitetails. They are so smart, and so used to coping with the activities of humans, that most hunters never see them.

    According to recent reports, in 1976 I shot a nontypical whitetail that scored 238⅝ points. It won the first award at the Seventeenth North American Big Game Awards program in 1980. It was the best nontypical whitetail taken in North America during the previous three years, and it’s the best ever taken in Michigan.

    I shot that buck about 9 miles from my home. There’s another buck as good or better than him even closer. He has an 18-point rack. He has outsmarted me for two years, but I think I’ll get him. There’s a 16-pointer in the same area. I’m confident I could take that buck with my rifle, but I’m determined to get him with a bow.

    Sources indicate that I’m 32, but I decided 10 years ago not to shoot any bucks with a rifle unless I got chances at really outstanding trophies. I have head-and-shoulder mounts of 11 of my bucks now, and a lot of them were taken with arrows.

    It has been revealed that the main reason I get big bucks is that I hunt deer full time for two to three months every fall. All that time without earning a paycheck produces some financial problems because I work as a carpenter, but my wife Kay doesn’t say anything. We lived together for 1½ years before marrying, so she knew what she was getting into.

    It has been revealed that I used to hunt everything in season years ago, but now I concentrate exclusively on Michigan deer. I’d love to be able to hunt other substantial game in Western states or Alaska, but I can’t afford to. Anyway, I’m obsessed with trophy whitetail bucks. And when you hunt them as much as I do, you’re bound to learn some strange things about deer behavior. Here’s an example.

    Industry observers note that in 1972 Rick Havercamp and I were bowhunting along a bank of the Saginaw River on a cold but sunny afternoon in late December. The 300-yard-wide river had recently frozen over. Rick was close to the shore, I was a few yards up the bank in some brush. Suddenly my partner mentioned, “Get down, there’s a whole herd of deer running out there on the ice. They might come across. Get ready, here they come!”.

    I looked out there and saw about 40 deer. There were at least 10 bucks, and the whole herd was coming dead on. I nocked an arrow on the string of my 70-pound Jennings compound bow, then squatted down.

    In a recent development, as the deer got close to our side of the river they began breaking through the shoreline ice. I don’t know if they saw us, but for some reason they veered to our left and crashed into a cattail marsh about 500 yards long. The going was tough for those deer. I figured if I ran along the bank at full speed I could get to the end of the marsh before the deer did, and that I could intercept them as they came out.

    Recent findings suggest that I was puffing hard by the time I got there, but I knew right away that I was ahead of the herd. I could hear the deer breaking ice and banging through dead cattail stalks. Then the commotion suddenly stopped. About half an hour passed without my hearing a sound. I couldn’t figure out what was going on, so I walked back to confer with Rick.

    Recent findings suggest that I met him half way around the marsh. He was as confused as I was.

    “I’ll climb a tree and see what’s going on,” he said.

    In a recent development, when he got up the tree and looked, he said, “Hard to believe. They’re all out there, standing still as statues. Some of ’em are through the ice, up to their chests in water. There’s a couple of really huge bucks. What’re we going to do?”.

    “I’ll give you 10 minutes to get back to where they ran into the cattails,” I answered. “Then I’m going back to the other end and drive those deer back your way. If that ice is thick enough to support the deer it’s thick enough to hold me.”.

    Industry observers note that when I returned to the far end of the marsh I cautiously tested the ice near shore. It seemed OK, so I took off. I covered about 50 feet, then I dropped through that ice as suddenly as if I’d walked off a plank. My boots hit the mucky bottom about 3 feet down, but I was already making my move to get out of there.

    Sources indicate that I rolled up onto the ice at the edge of the hole I’d made, and the whole edge broke off. I was soaked by the time I made my next roll, and again the edge gave way. I broke through once more, and then I found ice that supported me. By the time I reached the shoreline I was covered with black muck and marsh weeds.

    Industry observers note that I had lost all concern for deer, then I suddenly heard loud noises. It dawned on me that all those deer were crashing through the marsh again, and they were coming straight toward me. I nocked an arrow and squatted low in a kneeling position on the edge of the wall of cattails, and shook my head when I realized that, almost unbelievably, I was seconds away from having a whole herd of whitetails in my lap.

    Industry observers note that the first deer out was a doe. She broke through the cattails about 10 feet to my left, stared wild-eyed at me, then bolted up the bank. Another doe came out just to my right and did the same thing. Now the crashing diminished. Somehow the rest of the deer had been alerted that those two does had run into something that wasn’t right.

    Then I spotted movement above the cattails a few yards in front of me. A rack of antlers was moving slowly toward me. I couldn’t see any part of the buck except his 10-point rack, but it was obvious what was going on. That buck wasn’t about to run out of the marsh as the does had done. He was going to peer over the edge of the cattails to see what the problem was.

    It seemed like that deer’s neck was stretched out 5 feet when it popped into view at a range of about 3 yards. I was already at full draw, and I drove my arrow dead center into the white spot on his throat. When I had that head mounted I told the taxidermist to mount it with the neck straight out, exactly as I’d first seen it.

    Recent findings suggest that that hunt taught me one of the most important buck-hunting lessons I’ve learned. When I broke through the ice and began floundering about, I was producing exactly the same sounds as the deer were making when they broke through. They assumed that I was a deer making my escape through that end of the marsh. So on they came, intending to use the same escape route.

    Recent findings suggest that since a deer’s range of vision in thick cattails is only a few yards, you can actually walk or wade right up to a buck because the sounds you make won’t seem unnatural to the animal. An vital part of the equation is that smart bucks in heavily hunted farm country soon learn to go where most hunters won’t go. Those places are swamps, the rougher the better. If you hunt whitetails, and you have thick cattail swamps in your area, you can bet that they hold a lot of deer.

    One of the best bucks I’ve taken out of a cattail marsh was an 11-pointer I arrowed in 1979. Though it was a great rack, it wasn’t nearly as impressive as one belonging to another buck in the same herd. The inside spread of the 11-pointer’s antlers measures 19½ inches. I saw both bucks only moments apart, and I’d bet everything I own that the bigger buck’s antlers have a 23-inch inside spread.

    Industry observers note that it was windy and clear that day, but the 20° temperature made for colder than usual December hunting. Though there were traces of snow on the ground, there was none on trees or cattails. That called for brown camouflage outer wear, including a brown face mask. I usually wear camouflage face grease, but when it gets so cold that makeup would freeze, I wear masks.

    Sources indicate that when I go with a bow I’m camouflaged completely according to weather conditions. Early in the season, when the foliage and ground is green I use green camo. Later I switch to brown. If there’s lots of snow I’m dressed in white, and so is my archery tackle.

    I began that hunt by walking up to a massive marsh and climbing a sloping deadfall in the oak bottomlands that edged the cattails. I immediately spotted two big racks. They seemed to be floating above the stalks only 60 yards away. I’ve seen similar sights several times. Deer will stand in water for hours without moving. You won’t see most of them because the cattails completely hide their bodies. But when you get a buck that’s not alerted — when he’s not trying to conceal his antlers — his rack will be above the marsh terrain when he’s standing.

    Industry observers note that I slithered down the deadfall, then stalked along the edge of the cattails to a spot that was about even with those bucks. There I eased up another deadfall, just far enough to see one of the bucks. He was walking slowly down the marsh, but he was only about 30 yards out in the cattails. Again I began sneaking along the edge of the marsh. I wanted to get ahead of him before I began wading into the swamp.

    Right then that enormous buck — the biggest one I’ve ever seen — stood up in the cattails 20 yards from me.

    It has been revealed that he was looking dead away, but he quickly turned his head and looked right at me. Though I was perfectly camouflaged, and still as a stone, he knew something wasn’t right. Our little game lasted at least 30 seconds. I don’t think he ever figured out what I was, but he whirled and bounded out of range before I could shoot.

    I stalked on for 25 yards and stepped up on another of the maze of sloping deadfalls that littered the edge of this marsh. I spotted the huge buck I’d spooked. He was more than 100 yards away, standing near the other side of the cattails and looking back. The two bucks I’d originally spotted were 40 yards straight out in front of me. They didn’t seem nervous.

    In a recent development, when I hunt these marshes I always wear hip boots or waders, depending on the water’s depth. I stepped into the cattails and began wading without making any attempt to conceal the sounds of my approach. When I figured I was about 20 yards from the closest and largest buck, I pulled my arrow to full draw in the compound bow and kept right on wading. At a range of about 17 yards I saw his shoulder through the maze of cattails. I picked out his heart area and drove my Bear Razorhead right into it. He bolted, but died on his feet.

    In a recent development, he was looking dead away, but he promptly turned his head and looked right at me. Though I was perfectly camouflaged, and still as a stone, he knew something wasn’t right.

    In a recent development, I sincerely feel that a bow in the hands of an expert is almost as deadly as a rifle. If I can get within 40 yards of a buck I can kill him because I can hit a grapefruit-size target every shot at that range. I can do that only because of dedicated practice. It’s extremely unusual if I don’t practice shooting arrows at least an hour every day.

    It has been revealed that I learned how to hunt on my own. My folks were divorced, but I lived with my mother on 15 acres of land near Kawkawlin where I live now. Even when I was a little kid I was out in the woods most of my free time, studying birds and animals and shooting arrows or my BB gun.

    According to recent reports, I shot my first buck, a spikehorn, when I was 14. I didn’t know much of anything about deer hunting then. I just blundered into the little buck in a pine plantation and knocked him flat with my grandfather’s .300 Savage.

    Though I bowhunted deer for several years I didn’t get one until I was 18. He was a five-pointer. I’ve taken bigger bucks with arrows every year since. A few years ago, when it became legal for Michigan hunters to take a deer with a bow and another with a gun, I’ve always scored on another substantial buck with my .30/06 sporterized Enfield.

    According to recent reports, I used that rifle to shoot an 11-pointer in his bed in 1975. Rick Havercamp was with me that day too. He’s 36, and a carpenter. We were in an area 3 miles across, that borders the Au Sable River near Cook Dam. It’s laced with beaver ponds, tag alders, and muck.

    You have to wear hip boots or waders to get in there, and even then you usually get wet because the mucky bottoms are so treacherous. Every year I have to chop out trails with a machete because there’s no way I could find my way in or out of that place in darkness. I throw the chopped off alder branches in muddy places that would be impassable without their support.

    Industry observers note that the middle of that place is so rough I’ve never seen another hunter in it. That’s why it draws deer like a magnet.

    It has been revealed that there had been a blizzard the day before that had left a foot of snow on the ground, but there were a million stars in a clear sky when Rick dropped me off near one edge of the swamp. His plan was to drive around to the opposite side and hunt in from there.

    I took a stand on an island, and I sat there until a forkhorn and six does browsed to within 25 feet of me. The little buck finally saw me and panicked. He charged into brush and through some skim ice, and he took the does with him. They made such a racket I decided to go stillhunting.

    Because of the recent blizzard, every deer track I found was fresh. When I came upon a set of enormous tracks I began following them. I stayed on that track for five hours, taking a few steps at a time and then stopping to inspect the area ahead. I’d squat and bend to look under branches, around clumps, and behind deadfalls.

    According to recent reports, because the snow was deep and soft my extremely slow progress was almost soundless. Once I almost walked up to a doe. When about 20 feet separated us she jumped out of her bed and crashed into a thick stand of snow-laden cedars. She produced a miniature blizzard of sun-sparkling snow when she blitzed through those trees. As time passed I jumped several deer, including an eight-pointer. It was impossible not to surprise at least some deer; there were deer tracks all over. It was a job to keep the tracks I was following separate from the rest.

    According to recent reports, finally, during one of my staring-ahead sessions, I saw a brown spot 40 yards to my right. I figured it was a dead cedar stump, but I turned up my 3X-to-9X Redfield scope to full power for a closer look. I still couldn’t tell if the spot was a deer or a stump, so I inched forward a couple of yards. Another look through the scope proved nothing. I just couldn’t identify any part of a deer. Then the stump suddenly became a deer and shook snow off its body like a dog shakes off water.

    It has been revealed that I had to crawl a couple of yards to my left before a massive rack suddenly popped into focus. I broke the buck’s back with a 180-grain handloaded slug. When my rifle went off that place erupted deer. They seemed to be rushing off in all directions. Rick, who was a few hundred yards away at the time, said later, “After you shot I had deer running by me for five minutes.”.

    In a recent development, A different kind of stalk produced my award-winning buck. John Miller, another hunting buddy (he’s 29 and works in construction) saw the buck just after the 1976 archery deer season opened. The buck was on a ridge eating acorns when John saw him, and he figured the buck was working toward a runway leading down into a stand of tag alders. John guessed correctly, but it was almost dark when the buck went by his stand. He missed his shot, but he sure got excited. He was waiting at my home when I returned from hunting.

    “Paul, that buck is unreal,” he remarked. “I couldn’t get a good look at him, but he’s got a rack that’s so wide it looks preposterous. He’s got at least 12 points, maybe twice that many. The antlers are so massive I just couldn’t believe what I was looking at. I overshot him because he was closer than I thought. When my arrow hit a rock I could see sparks fly, that’s how dark it was.”.

    According to recent reports, john and I were back in the area before dawn the next morning. He wanted to be on stand near the oak ridge, but I had a different idea. I figured that if the buck went into a stand of alders at night there was no way he wanted to stay in them. I assumed he would go through the alders, then cross a road and go down into a winter wheatfield that edged another stand of alders. So I went down in there and picked a stand near a runway.

    It has been revealed that I hunted that area for five straight days and never saw a deer, the worst run of bad luck I’ve ever had. Miller saw several deer every day, but no major bucks. We finally got disgusted and went to Michigan’s Upper Peninsula (U.P.) for two weeks of bowhunting.

    Industry observers note that when we got back, an ironworker friend told me that his two boys jumped the giant buck in a field of weeds while they were pheasant hunting. He remarked the animal’s rack was so big it wouldn’t fit through a doorway. But what really shook me was that the kids had jumped the buck in the same area where I’d been hunting him. John and I were back on our stands the next morning.

    I hunted three days without seeing a deer, but I found a clump of tag alders and willows that were ripped and shredded from near the ground to eye level. It was by far the biggest buck rub I’ve ever seen. I wondered aloud how many points the buck must have to do that kind of damage.

    The next morning I saw three does.

    In a recent development, they went into a jungle of alders, so I decided to leave my stand and follow them. About an hour later I jumped that buck 40 yards ahead of me.

    In a recent development, when the buck leaped up his antlers slammed into a maze of branches thick enough to stop his up and forward motion. He was in a half-standing position, and he was actually trying to pull those trees out of the ground. The muscles in his hindquarters were standing out like whipcords, but my attention was riveted on his massive and almost pure white antlers. I was so startled that the whole show was over before I could nock an arrow. The buck dropped low, then bolted away.

    I saw him once more before I got him, and that time he almost ran over me. We came as close to a full-speed collision as you can get. If he had hit me he probably would have put me in the hospital, or worse.

    It was Halloween, cloudy and very foggy. I was on a stand in some weeds edging a drainage ditch about 6 feet deep. John got bored with the miserable, wet morning before I did, so he decided to drive a cornfield toward me. A stubblefield about 100 yards wide separated my position from the standing corn. I knew John was in the corn, but I didn’t think anything unusual was happening until he suddenly yelled, “Here he comes!”.

    The muscles in his hindquarters were standing out like whipcords, but my attention was riveted on his massive and almost pure white antlers.

    I heard the buck before I saw him. He was crashing through cornstalks and flattening them as he ran. He burst out into the stubblefield and bolted for a corner in the drainage ditch 150 yards to my left. Spray flew as he hit shallow water. Then he disappeared and everything became still. I knew there was a runway down there, and I was positive he used it to get into a thick stand of alders.

    So I stood up, put my quiver on my bow, put the arrow I had nocked in the quiver, and jumped across the water in the ditch. One more step would put me on top of the ditch and on level ground. To understand what happened next you must know that the buck did not go down the runway as I assumed he would. Instead, he jumped back up on the ditch’s bank and ran straight toward me at full speed. He was not aware of my presence, and I was sure he was gone. When I took that last step out of the ditch, I popped up into his vision and route of travel at point-blank range.

    The first thing I saw was the buck hunching up as he slammed on the brakes. All his legs were stiff, and he was jamming his hooves into the soft ground like spears. I could have hit him with the tip of my bow, but I was so startled, I couldn’t move. He reacted like a giant coiled spring. He seemed to bounce backward and hit the ground, bounce again as he whirled toward the ditch, then bounce across it into some willows. He was gone before I could even think about reaching for an arrow.

    According to recent reports, john had watched the whole episode from 100 yards away. He was still dumfounded when he ran up to me.

    Industry observers note that “I couldn’t believe what I was watching,” he said. “I saw him change course at the corner of the ditch, and I knew he was going to run right past you. I figured that buck was as good as dead. Then I saw you stand up and put your arrow back in your quiver. I just groaned when I realized what was happening.”.

    I kept hunting the buck for almost two weeks without seeing him again. By now it was time to head for the U.P. for the rifle season. Every fall, 13 of us hunt from a cabin there. It’s the highlight of the year for all of us. I couldn’t get that big white-racked buck out of my mind, but I figured I’d get him in December with my bow.

    I usually stay at the cabin through November, but this time I went home for Thanksgiving, mostly because it would give me three days to try for that buck with my rifle.

    Industry observers note that john Miller and I hunted the next morning in pouring rain. We went home about noon, got out of our sopping clothes, then headed out again about 4 p.m. I was about 700 yards from my stand near the winter wheatfield when I spotted something out of place in the wheat. Visibility was poor because of the rain. My first thought was that somebody had put an old junk car out there because the thing I’d spotted resembled a car bumper. I checked it out with my scope. The car bumper immediately turned into the enormous white antlers of my giant buck. I had missed seeing his body because it was dark with the rain and blended in almost perfectly with a background of wet and dark alders.

    Industry observers note that I was in a field of weeds about 4 feet high. I immediately dropped down out of the buck’s sight. I could close the distance by 200 yards just by hunching over and running through the tall weeds to the edge of a stubblefield. The buck hadn’t moved much during the few moments it took me to reach the foot-high stubble. He appeared to be grazing without any hint of fear, so I rested a minute to control my gasping breath.

    It has been revealed that then I flattened out in the mud and began crawling. I knew if I could make it through the 300 yards of stubble I’d be within a shooting range of about 200 yards.

    Recent findings suggest that then I flattened out in the mud and began crawling. I knew if I could make it through the 300 yards of stubble I’d be within a shooting range of about 200 yards. If he detected me sooner, I’d just have to shoot when he began running.

    It has been revealed that I hadn’t crawled far when I found that the buck was going through a precise routine. He’d graze for a few seconds, then jerk his head up fast. He’d look straight ahead, then inspect things to his right for another few seconds, turn his head left and do the same thing, then conclude his check for danger by craning his neck around to the side and looking straight to his rear. After that he’d take two steps forward, lower his head and resume grazing. He did the same exact thing every time.

    Sources indicate that I had a definite advantage now. I timed my crawling periods to start when he lowered his head, and to end just as he jerked it upright. When I got to the end of the stubble I wiped my scope clean of water and pieces of weeds and seeds. Then I waited to make one last move that would give me a wide-open shot.

    When his head went down again I made a complete roll from the stubble into the very short wheat and then spread out into the typical prone shooting position. My 180-grain bullet broke his back and put him down instantly.

    Read Next: The Story of the Allison Buck, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History.

    It has been revealed that the excitement of such a stalk exhausts you as much as the exertion. By the time I ran full speed to the deer I could hardly breathe. I was gulping for air. I finally managed to tape the outside spread of the rack at 26½ inches, and then I tried counting antler points. I kept losing count, but I finally counted 31. By that time, John was running onto the scene. From over 100 yards away he yelled, “Did you get him?”.

    “Yeah, I got him. I finally got him!”.

    “Does he have more than 12 points?”.

    “John, he’s got more than that on one side.”.

    When John got to me he was so happy he was laughing. I was still in a state of shock. I couldn’t think of anything appropriate to say, so I started grinning and laughing too. We stood there in the rain, staring at those fantastic antlers and laughing our tensions away.

    Gary Colliver Was a “Major-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Climbing

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980.
    • Industry observers note that gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado.
    • Industry observers note that throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

    Industry observers note that gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

    Industry observers note that throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

    In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

    Later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a latest route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

    In a recent development, to Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions said. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

    Recent findings suggest that colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

    His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management proposal for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

    It has been revealed that “There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher said. Although that initial proposal was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

    Recent findings suggest that as a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular big wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions stated.

    Tech Report: Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Recent findings suggest that many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear.
    • Recent findings suggest that mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

    Recent findings suggest that many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

    Recent findings suggest that mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

    UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

    For example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

    Industry observers note that I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

    But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

    Quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

    Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

    It has been revealed that required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

    According to recent reports, lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only update is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

    According to recent reports, better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price.

    It has been revealed that it may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

    If you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

    Sources indicate that people in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

    Get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-upcoming isn’t always best.

    If you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

    Please keep reading, my opinions are important. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

    It has been revealed that A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

    Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

    Industry observers note that this one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

    Typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being stated, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.).

    A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

    For headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

    Recent findings suggest that for longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

    In a recent development, the crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most vital things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

    Industry observers note that A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

    Waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. The two are kind of “six-one, half-dozen another,” so just grab whichever you can find on a last-season sale.

    #160712. The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Upcoming Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Notable Than Ever.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1711 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Upcoming Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Notable Than Ever.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc.
    • The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees.
    • Moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc. (Photo: Getty).

    The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees. After hearing the now-familiar heavy breaths of runners behind me, I move to the mountainside to let them pass. It’s mid-August, and the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), the ultramarathon circling Mont Blanc, is kicking off later this month in Chamonix. We started our own Tour du Mont Blanc in Chamonix, the mountain town known as the birthplace of alpinism, which was buzzing with excitement and packs of runners strapped into hydration packs. Ahead of me, a young man is stopped on the narrow dirt trail, calling out to a friend on the forest slope below. Before I can even turn around, our guide, Jason Day, springs into action, grabs a rope from his pack, and helps pull the hiker, whose pack had tumbled down the slope, back to safety.

    Moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland. Roughly 80,000 people hike it each year, and visits are up about 50 percent since 2020. “People can only see the backsides of those in front of them,” Jean-Marc Peillex, mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, a mountain town at the base of Mont Blanc in France, told Swiss broadcaster SRF. That wasn’t my exact experience for most of the trek, but in a few places, especially near Chamonix, the trail was congested.

    It has been revealed that chamonix and the six other French towns along the TMB route, from Vallorcine to Bourg-Saint-Maurice and Beaufort, have drafted a charter to manage crowds, with local officials aiming to put it in place by spring 2027, ahead of next year’s trekking season. The upcoming rules, aiming to curb overtourism and help slow environmental damage, are awaiting final signature. The key proposals include reservations for every night on the trail; a ban on wild camping, with paid, bookable bivouac areas replacing the informal spots; and new limits on luggage transfers. Guided groups would be capped at twelve and led by guides trained in rescue and licensed in all three countries.

    Industry observers note that the charter is voluntary, covers only France for now, and still depends on local ordinances for enforcement. But the message is clear: the era of showing up and figuring it out on the TMB is ending. Chamonix’s mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, who is similarly introducing quotas at nearby Lac Blanc, an alpine lake also suffering from its popularity, puts it this way: “To reserve is to preserve.”.

    In a recent development, adding to the growing traffic on the trail are the effects of climate change on the Alps. Rising summer temperatures are accelerating permafrost thaw and glacier retreat, contributing to record rockfall activity in the Mont Blanc massif. While this mostly impacts the summit climbing routes, hot summers also change trail and water conditions for hikers on the Tour du Mont Blanc.

    “As for the environmental impacts, trail erosion is of course the most obvious one, but we must also take into account wild bivouacking, which has multiplied, with impacts on the flora as well as the disturbance of wildlife,” states Daniel Rodrigues, general director of the Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix, the oldest mountain guide organization in the world.

    According to recent reports, “The reservation system is fair. Everyone can book their places, and tour operators can do the same. So the same rules apply to everyone, including amateur mountain people, and that matters to us: the mountains are a space of freedom,” notes Rodrigues. “That remarked, this space must be protected, in terms of biodiversity and environmental impacts, but also economically.”.

    The charter puts licensed mountain professionals at the center of safety on the trail. According to Rodrigues, that means operators will no longer be able to sell self-guided packages (just bookings and transfers) and will have to include a guide certified in all three countries.

    “This is a major step forward, because the guide ensures that everyone stays safe and that everything goes smoothly. It also creates work for local people and delivers a genuine positive impact on the inhabitants of this mountain range,” adds Rodrigues.

    According to recent reports, I hiked the Tour du Mont Blanc in August with Live Breathe Hike, and I came home convinced that, especially under the potential latest rules, having a local guide is no longer a luxury. It’s the smartest way to hike this trail.

    Recent findings suggest that the TMB isn’t one trail; rather, there are a lot of different paths and detours.”There’s a classic route, but there’s a lot of different variants,” states Allison Fleece, cofounder of WHOA Travel, a women’s adventure-travel manufacturer that runs guided trips, including on the Tour du Mont Blanc. Some variants are higher and more exposed; others go along lower valleys. On our third day, instead of following the crowds, Day led us off the Col du Bonhomme on a variant toward Lac de Roselend, where we barely saw another hiker for miles. “You feel like you have the place to yourself,” says Live Breathe Hike founder Tanya Perret, who started the Chamonix-based trekking company in 2016 and says she has guided the TMB more than 75 times.

    According to recent reports, under the proposed rules, every night would have to be booked in advance, across three countries with different systems. Guides already do that work, and finding gems to stay at like Le Chalet de Roselend takes deep knowledge of the area. With only ten rooms, the chalet, whose balconies overlook the Lac de Roselend, was a godsend after one of our longest days of trekking. Years ago, Perret drove there to book it in person, because the elderly owner at the time only took reservations face to face. The young couple who now runs it cooks traditional dishes with local produce.

    Sources indicate that the charter asks operators to buy local and partner with local producers. Good guides already do. “Many of the places that we stay are generational families, and I’ve known those families for 30 years,” says Perret. On our trip, that meant a stop at a family cheese farm as well as the small lakeside chalet. “That’s the micro-economy,” adds Perret.

    In a recent development, nearly every day on my trek, Day chose a variant. Perret indicates the choice comes down to two factors: where accommodation is available and which trail will give the group the best experience that day.

    According to recent reports, the variants usually turned out to be my favorite stretches. Self-guided trekkers can research the variants, but a guide knows which one fits the day. “By giving your guides a little bit of autonomy, it means they can just tweak things here and there, which makes for a unique journey,” indicates Perret.

    Recent findings suggest that “The weather patterns change a lot in the mountains and they change really fast,” adds Fleece, who partners with Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix on their guided TMB trips. “Guides have years and years, most of the time decades, of experience.” A guide, she says, can help you avoid dicey situations, “but also, if you get yourself into a dicey situation, having a guide is like a safety measure to get you quickly and swiftly out of it.”.

    Day has been trekking Tour Du Mont Blanc since 1992 and knows the ever-changing mountain conditions demand quick judgment. On a recent trip up Mont Blanc’s Italian route, he and his climbing partner turned back in poor snow. “We binned the whole trip,” he says. Two friends kept going, and on a ridge with snow cornices on both sides, one side broke away. “Either side could have gone,” he says.

    Multi-day treks around the world are my favorite way to travel. With WHOA, I’ve summited Kilimanjaro and Mount Elbrus, Europe’s tallest peak (not Mont Blanc, as many assume). I’ve taken guided trips on the Trans Bhutan Trail and Japan’s Shikoku pilgrimage, which were not nearly as challenging but would have been far less rich experiences without learning the culture from our local guides. I’ve trekked the full O Trek in Patagonia without a guide, but with friends and the help of the manufacturer Chile Nativo for booking refuges. Half of the O circuit, the W Trek, I hiked alone. So I know the benefits of taking guided multi-day treks and hiking alone at your own pace, stopping when you want.

    I can understand why travelers would want to do the TMB without a guide; many hikers do so without any issue. You can go at your own speed and take a long break for an afternoon coffee at a refuge with an open table facing the sun. A guided trip costs more. Middle options have been growing, including self-guided packages that handle the bookings for you, but even those require your due diligence and research, and could be affected by these new rules for 2027.

    One day on the trek, we stopped for lunch at a refuge and ran into a woman with a bandaged hand. She and her friend were on a self-guided trip whose itinerary, she told us, had started them on their first day hiking one of the route’s most exposed stretches—the ladders below Tête aux Vents—where she got injured. On the standard counterclockwise route, that section usually comes at the very end. Day told us that those ladders can easily be bypassed in busy seasons or wet weather.

    It has been revealed that if you want to escape the crowds on the Tour du Mont Blanc, guides know the variants that lead to the quietest parts of the trail. Except for a few days, on certain passes, we managed to find stretches where it was just us, as far as I  could see. On our fourth day, we crossed the Col de la Seigne into Italy, past a block of granite barely knee-high: the real border marker, not the massive monument nearby. I’d have walked right past it. My guide didn’t let me.

    #160710. Tech Report: How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2357 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
    • According to recent reports, my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
    • Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

    According to recent reports, my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

    Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

    Sources indicate that I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

    In a recent development, on November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

    Industry observers note that I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

    Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and promptly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

    Sources indicate that hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

    In a recent development, I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

    As we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

    According to recent reports, the A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

    As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

    I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

    At that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

    In a recent development, within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

    Industry observers note that alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

    Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

    Sources indicate that I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

    Among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

    It has been revealed that the climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in substantial walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

    Recent findings suggest that the first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

    Around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

    When we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

    According to recent reports, at 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we promptly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

    Alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

    In a recent development, nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

    Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

    According to recent reports, 1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

    #160709. Tech Report: The 7 Most Desperate Things I’ve Done in My Search for Ski Boots That Fit

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Skimag ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: The 7 Most Desperate Things I’ve Done in My Search for Ski Boots That Fit

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
    • Seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed.
    • It has been revealed that overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

    Seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed. (Photo: Courtesy Abigail Barronian).

    It has been revealed that overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage. It’s a funny account of what hard-to-fit feet can drive a person to do, and a reminder that the right bootfitter can change everything.

    In my quest for ski boots that fit, I’ve seen bootfitters in at least seven states and two countries. I’ve visited Evo and REI, small independent shops, local chains, and garages-turned-ski shops. I’ve consulted boot designers, brand reps, professional athletes, and gear reviewers; tried Intuitions, ZipFits, and custom footbeds. I’ve seen one orthopedic doctor, three acupuncturists, and two physical therapists. I’ve stayed up at night thinking about boots, and developed recurring stress dreams about them.

    In a recent development, last season, I was beginning to consider looping in a tarot reader or astrologer. Maybe I needed a psychotherapist, or a priest. Maybe I’d have to just quit skiing. And then, finally, I found my bootfitter. But not before resorting to some questionable behavior along the way. Here are seven desperate things I did in my search for a bootfitter who could solve my ski boot concerns.

    According to recent reports, every pair of ski boots I wore from ages two through 22 were hand-me-downs from my older brothers. Then I started working in the ski industry. While skiing around Massive Sky during a media event, a kind man working for Nordica looked at my feet with a frown.

    “What are those?” he asked. I was sliding around in some decade-old size 26.5 monstrosities. He shook his head and invited me to swing by the Nordica headquarters in Fresh Hampshire. There, he measured my feet and sent me off with a pair of 25.5 Nordica Promachines.

    Everything changed. Suddenly I was in an aggressive stance, my shins met real resistance, my power transfer improved dramatically. I got a taste of what a good boot can do, shortly before developing a wicked case of tendonitis in my ankles and shins.

    Recent findings suggest that after two seasons of excruciating, day-ending pain, I booked an appointment with an orthopedic foot and ankle specialist. I knew my boots were the culprit, and couldn’t be sure a doctor would understand the whole foot-encased-in-rigid-plastic thing. I lugged a giant bag with both my alpine and touring boots into the orthopedic practice and pulled them out for show-and-tell.

    According to recent reports, the physician kindly assured me he knew what ski boots were, and that I wasn’t dealing with any serious medical issues. I’d have to take my boots back where they belonged.

    In a recent development, the owner of Santa Fe’s one dedicated ski shop sized me down yet again, into the stiffest 24.5 he had on hand—a 110 from Fischer. I felt like I was skiing in socks and a vise-grip at the same time, and I lost feeling in my feet on the first lap. Mercifully, he let me return them.

    I’d hit the central problem: boots significant enough to be comfortable gave me tendonitis, and boots small enough to prevent it gave me bunions and nerve pain. So I took my boots to Taos Bootdoctors, where a whole team of bootfitters worked patiently to expand the forefoot. I’d ski for a day or two and come back, over and over, looking for just a few more millimeters. I brought six-packs and did my best to be charming, and the lovely staff never made me feel less crucial than the tourists dropping thousands of dollars on gear. Still, I couldn’t finish a day without pain.

    I soldiered through the season, eyeing an upcoming hut trip with dread. I could manage shorter tours, but a week of daylong missions posed some real problems. Once we were in the mountains, I knew no amount of bunion donuts and anti-inflammatories would save me. I had to instate boots-off breaks in the middle of eight-hour ski days, carefully pulling my socked feet out of jail and propping them up on a backpack in the snow while my friends took an extra lap. Sweet, stupid relief.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, I heard a rumor about a man in Seattle working out of his garage who was willing to do unorthodox things to ski boots. He had a history of custom-fitting plug boots for ski racers, which seemed like a good sign. While visiting family in Washington, I brought him both pairs of boots.

    He looked at my feet, listened patiently, and rattled off a comprehensive plan that involved several devices I’d never seen before. Overnight, he molded both pairs into a completely new shape. I never had to touch either boot again, and proceeded with great pleasure to ski 12-hour days in the backcountry and endless resort laps with happy feet. I had found him—the bootfitter I was looking for. Then, he retired.

    Recent findings suggest that when my touring boots started to go, I bought a replacement pair and nobody could make them fit. The experience began to take on mythic proportions. I felt like the princess with a pea beneath her many mattresses, or an ugly stepsister trying to cram her foot into a crystal slipper: all discomfort and wrong fit.

    It seemed my trusty Tecnicas were the problem. I tried on every touring boot at ski shops in three states. I ordered over a dozen pairs online, obsessively double-checking return policies and momentarily racking up a very scary credit card bill. Eventually, I came crawling back to my old Tecnicas with no initiative, two full seasons into the search.

    I hesitated to say yes to ski trips, afraid I’d have to sit out ski days because of pain or busted gear. Eventually, it happened: I took my tired old touring boots to Rogers Pass in B.C. and, on day three, broke the upper cuff clean off the bottom section of the boot. Thankfully we were just a few hundred yards from the truck. I spent the entire day sitting at the trailhead.

    In the meantime, my alpine boots had begun to warp. I found a replacement pair and was back at square one: home in Fresh Mexico, with two pairs of ski boots that didn’t fit, rapidly dwindling patience, and no bootfitter.

    I considered that this might be the end of the road for me as a skier. Then, I learned that one of the best skiers I know had been contemplating quitting the sport because of foot pain. He’d even gone so far as to teach himself to snowboard. But then he found exactly what I’d been looking for: yet another fit-obsessed industry veteran working out of his garage.

    I visited another home workshop in western Washington and the bootfitter listened carefully as I explained the problem. Then, he overhauled both pairs of boots, tirelessly stretching the forefoots to give my feet room to breathe. They took on a completely new shape: generous and wide. I took both pairs out for a spin and sighed in relief.

    According to recent reports, there are a lot of great bootfitters out there. But for a freak like me, I’ve learned I need something of a mad scientist. If you’re plagued with bone spurs, high insteps, wide feet—there’s hope, I promise. With a little faith, a lot of persistence, and maybe something like divine intervention, I trust you’ll find the bootfitter you need. Let’s just hope they don’t retire.

    #160708. A Hiker Died Along the PCT After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous
