    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    The Best Spots to Choose-and-Cut Your Own Christmas Tree This Year

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You know the scene from National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation.
    • In a recent development, while you cannot simply waltz into any forest and begin chopping down trees, you can absolutely fulfill your dreams of being your own Clark Griswold this festive season.
    • These permits range from $5 to $20, and they’re as much of a win for the woods as for those wanting an authentic Clark Griswold experience.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You know the scene from National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation. Clark Griswold, played by comedian Chevy Chase, is on a quest to provide an unforgettable holiday for his family when he leads his less-than-enthused wife and kids into the snowy woods, his eyes gleaming with excitement. He’s on a mission to find the Christmas tree of all Christmas trees. This classic holiday movie is almost 40 years old, but the drive to cut down your own tree is still very much alive today.

    In a recent development, while you cannot simply waltz into any forest and begin chopping down trees, you can absolutely fulfill your dreams of being your own Clark Griswold this festive season. Instead of buying a tree from a lot in town, choose-and-cut Christmas tree farms and a special U.S. Forest Service permit program allow you to do as the name suggests: find your own tree and cut it down yourself.

    These permits range from $5 to $20, and they’re as much of a win for the woods as for those wanting an authentic Clark Griswold experience.

    “In the West, one of our biggest challenges is wildfire risk,” Marcus Selig, chief conservation officer for the National Forest Foundation, tells Outside. “When you’re cutting a Christmas tree [through this permit program], you’re cutting out the small trees that create what we call ladder fuel, so thinning out those little trees and allowing the significant trees to have the resources they need to grow bigger and stronger and more fire resilient is good.”.

    Selig claims this thinning out trees is something the National Forest Foundation and U.S. Forest Service spends thousands of dollars per-acre to accomplisheach year, so allowing people to cut Christmas trees helps that cause. Cutting down smaller trees can also help improve wildlife habitat and the other trees around it.

    “With climate concerns, trees are more and more stressed as we go through droughts,” Selig explains. “Cutting out the small trees is like weeding a garden and means the substantial trees can do better.”.

    Industry observers note that some choose-and-cut farms also lean into sustainability using a regenerative farming method called coppicing, where a portion of the tree’s trunk and a branch or two are left after it’s cut down, stimulating latest growth. A new tree can sprout up from the same trunk and can do so over and over again.

    Industry observers note that “We have a few stumps that you can see where they’ve been regrown at least nine times,” Christy Carico, farm manager at Crest Ranch Tree Farm in Santa Cruz, California, tells Outside. Carico refers to the method, one her family uses on their farm, as “stump culture.”.

    For your own choose-and-cut adventure, these eight spots have plenty of holiday cheer and even more fir, cypress, pine, and spruce Christmas trees, among other varieties, to choose from. Just double-check your ceiling heights before you head out, and check for any pesky stowaway squirrels before bringing your tree home.

    Recent findings suggest that roughly 300,000 people participate in this true Clark Griswold experience—the U.S. Forest Service Christmas Tree Permit Program—each season, a program that requires you to trek into a national forest, choose and cut your tree with a hand saw, and haul it back to your car on your own.

    Pay attention to the areas each forest has designated for this program, and select a tree that will help thin out the forest, not one that’s standing alone.

    In a recent development, selig recommends strapping the tree on top of your car with the trunk closest to the front windshield to get it home. That way, the wind will flow with the direction the branches are lying, reducing any potential for damage.

    It has been revealed that “It’s amazing what trees can take,” Selig states. “They’re made to withstand strong winds in the wild, so they’ll be all right.”.

    Sources indicate that what’s the best benefit of opting for a choose-and-cut Christmas tree? “You know exactly where your tree came from and know it’s fresh,” says Tim Nieman, COO for the John T. Nieman Nursery. “These trees will last way longer than a tree you buy at a lot that’s been pre-cut probably one or two months ago.”.

    About 5,000 families tromp through this choose-and-cut Christmas tree farm about 30 minutes north of Cincinnati during the holidays. You can fell your own tree or have one of the team members, likely one of the roughly 25 Nieman family members who help out for the season, do it.

    In a recent development, red Barn Tree Farm has 40 acres of Fraser fir Christmas trees and sits adjacent to Linville Falls Winery near Boone, North Carolina. The Wiseman family has owned the property since 1998 and has always operated a choose-and-cut farm on it. In 2012, they opened the winery’s tasting room.

    “Our family joke is that we always encourage customers to pick their tree first before they visit the winery next door, or else their ceilings start getting taller,” claims co-owner Lindsay Wiseman.

    Recent findings suggest that hop on a hayride from the base of the farm up the hill to start your search. After choosing the perfect tannenbaum, their team will do the honors of cutting it down.

    According to recent reports, shell’s Christmas Tree Farm grows eight different tree varieties across 20 acres, including the blue ice cypress and Virginia pine, and has been selling trees for four decades. All of these species are able to grow in warmer weather as opposed to popular Christmas tree varieties like the Fraser fir, which need much cooler temperatures to thrive.

    The farm typically doesn’t officially open until close to Thanksgiving, but eager customers can go ahead and visit to tag their dream tree before the season starts for a small fee.

    In a recent development, maple Row Farm is a family-owned and run choose-and-cut farm that has been growing Christmas trees for over 100 years. Now, according to general manager and ninth-generation farmer Scott Edwards, the 250-acre farm has a “few hundred thousand trees” at any given time. They grow nine different varieties, from white spruce trees to Fraser fir and Norway spruce trees.

    Industry observers note that during the holiday season, the farm is as known for its tailgating as it is for its trees. It’s a quirky tradition that’s just as much a must-do for customers as is choosing their own tree. “People come and bring their neighborhood, or sports team, or friends,” Edwards states. “They’ll make food and usually bring a good selection of drinks as well. It’s different, but a cool thing.”.

    Choose-and-cut Christmas trees are only part of the allure of Spring Creek Growers, a southeast Texas family-owned farm. Plan on making a day trip out of it if you have little ones; the epic treehouse and hayrides are must-dos, and you can buy s’mores kits from the on-site bakery to make over one of their outdoor fire pits.

    During the holidays, the farm offers experiences such as doughnuts with Santa[[,]]and Tinsel and Tackle, a fishing experience for the littles.

    Everything is bigger in Texas, and the same goes for Spring Creek’s trees: this year, customers can find Christmas trees up to 13 feet tall to take home.

    The Rocks Christmas Tree Farm sits on 1,400 acres that were gifted to the Society for the Protection of Latest Hampshire Forests in 1978, with the condition that the land always be used for crops. When Nigel Manley, senior outreach manager for The Rocks and a farmer himself, started working there in 1986, it was a dairy farm. But it transitioned to growing trees shortly after he arrived.

    “We decided on choose-and-cut Christmas trees as the crop because it would bring people to a conserved property,” Manley states. They used to plant 7,000 upcoming trees a year, but Manley says warmer and wetter conditions as a result of climate change have meant scaling back to just 2,000. Keeping the former scale would have meant needing extensive field drainage or building raised beds.

    Any profits from tree sales go back into things like educational programs and conservation efforts for the society.

    Industry observers note that california’s oldest Christmas tree farm, Crest Ranch, has been operating since 1948 and has been owned by the same family all 70-plus years. It’s such a beloved part of the community that even in the wake of the devastating CZU Lightning Complex wildfire that swept through the Santa Cruz Mountains in 2020 and destroyed much of the property, people still came to buy their trees.

    “We were about to throw in the towel,” Carico says, “but our customers pushed us through post-fire and came that year and bought burnt trees to show their support.”.

    It has been revealed that the farm has started to recover, but there are still sections of their fields that will remain closed this season, limiting how many trees they’ll be able to sell. Post-fire, Carico and her team planted a host of Monterey fir trees, endemic to the area and a fast-growing variety, but customers will also find species like white firs and Arizona cypresses available.

    Recent findings suggest that washington is known as “The Evergreen State” due to its abundant forests, making it a natural spot for Christmas trees to shine. There are a number of national forests across the state, including Olympic, Gifford Pinchot, and Mount Baker-Snoqualmie, that offer Christmas tree permits if you’re feeling up for a walk in the woods.

    If not, there is an abundance of U-pick farms, too. Buttonwood Farm says they are the state’s only 100 percent certified organic Christmas tree farm and that they don’t use any chemicals to manage the farm.

    You can schedule an appointment to choose and cut your tree, but walk-ins are also welcome. For the ultimate experience, you can go to the farm, pick the perfect tree, and then have their team deliver it to your house.

    #160679. Remembering Chris Falkenstein, Long-time Yosemite Climber and Photographer

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (939 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    Remembering Chris Falkenstein, Long-time Yosemite Climber and Photographer

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors.
    • According to recent reports, chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer.
    • Sources indicate that I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors. (Photo: Courtesy Falkenstein Family Collection).

    According to recent reports, chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer. Better known by many as Falky, Finkelstein, Steiny, Schwackenstein, or Commando, Chris wore many hats throughout his life: devoted husband and father, loyal friend, accomplished climber, photographer, skier, whitewater kayaker, windsurfer, mountain biker, self-proclaimed computer nerd, and passionate lover of Yosemite and the outdoors.

    Sources indicate that I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport. I enjoyed it, but pursued other sports. In a way, I don’t think I’ve found a climbing partner that was ever as dialed as he was. My Dad was so quiet and humble about his achievements; there were so many things he never mentioned. I remember being out climbing with him, when he would tell some story like, “We were out here in the ‘80s, blasting a boom box and climbing.” It turns out, he would be talking about a first ascent.

    Those who knew him will remember his adventurous spirit, his enthusiasm for life, and the joy he found in exploring the world around him. His love for the outdoors was infectious. And the memories he created along the way will live on in those fortunate enough to have shared in his adventures.

    It has been revealed that when Chris arrived in Yosemite in 1972, he brought a foundation of climbing experience from the Gunks of Newly introduced York. His natural athleticism, determination, and enthusiasm quickly drew him into the dynamic and evolving climbing scene of Yosemite Valley. What began as an introduction to the Yosemite climbing community grew into a lifelong passion and a lasting legacy.

    He once remarked, “So off I went at 18 to explore climbing in Yosemite. Best decision of my life, and a true highlight… I consider my life beginning after 18. Stay young at heart forever if you can.”.

    Chris spent the remainder of his life in and around Yosemite, calling many places home over the years, including Camp 4, the Annex, Badger Pass, Sonora, Tuolumne Meadows, and El Portal. Eventually, he settled in Foresta, where he and his wife, Doe, retired to the home they built together.

    In a recent development, throughout his years in Yosemite, Chris became a respected presence in the climbing community, known for being a quiet and humble force. He established multiple first ascents in Yosemite Valley and Tuolumne Meadows. Among his notable first ascents were Do or Fly (5.11c), The Speed of Life (5.11b), Black Angel (5.11a), and Highway Star (5.10a). Along with Don Reid, he co-authored Rock Climbs of Tuolumne Meadows, first published in 1983. Four additional editions later followed. He also authored Yosemite Sport Climbs in 1992. Through his climbs, guidebooks, and contributions to the community, Chris helped shape and document Yosemite’s rich climbing history.

    According to recent reports, beyond his physical accomplishments in climbing, he inspired others and expanded the appreciation for the outdoors through his photography, videography, and online content. He captured the many aspects of climbing, mountaineering, and skiing, while sharing the extraordinary beauty of Yosemite.

    Chris’s work appeared in a wide range of publications, climbing guides, gear catalogs, climbing films, commercials, Hollywood productions, and websites. Chris’s photography became a familiar part of the Yosemite landscape itself. As Don Reid once remarked with a teasing smirk, “You know you are made with Yosemite photography when your photos appear on the Coke machines, shuttle buses, and climbing guide covers of the place.”.

    When it was too cold to climb, Chris also had a deep love for winter sports. He played hockey throughout his life and contributed to the local pick up hockey club in Yosemite. Alongside Bruce Brossman and Loyd Price, Chris completed the first single-day trans-Sierra ski trip via Tioga Pass. His name also lives on through several first descents in the Sierras, including the Solstice Couloir and Powerhouse Chute.

    At Badger Pass Ski Resort, Chris spent many years serving as ski patrol manager. He brought his knowledge of climbing techniques into ski patrol training, developing methods for chairlift rescues and assisting with backcountry rescue efforts. His impact was perhaps best captured by a skier he helped, who later described him as “an angel emerging from the woods.”.

    Recent findings suggest that early in his career, Chris worked for the Yosemite Climbing School, teaching climbing during the summer months and cross-country skiing in winter. He enjoyed summers as the employee housing manager in Tuolumne Meadows. In retirement, Chris continued to explore and enjoy the Sierras, while taking great pride in perfecting the art of being a grandfather. Chris also became an unofficial voice of Yosemite locals, keeping friends and former park residents connected to the place they loved by sharing updates and insights into the ever-changing landscape of Yosemite.

    Chris loved everything Yosemite. He devoted much of his time to documenting not only the climbing, skiing, and athletic pursuits that made the park famous, but also its immense beauty, extensive history, and the development and change over time. With an eye for the extraordinary as well as the everyday, he captured the moments, places, and details that might otherwise go unnoticed. Through his lens and storytelling, Chris shared his deep appreciation for Yosemite. In so doing, he preserved a piece of its story for others.

    Chris is survived by his wife Doe, his son Alex, his daughter-in-law Danielle, and his two-and-a-half-year-old grandson Finn, who loves trying to climb up anything in his path.

    #160678. Tech Report: These Ski Resorts Let You Ski for Free on the Day You Arrive

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (908 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Skimag ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: These Ski Resorts Let You Ski for Free on the Day You Arrive

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, november 28, 2023; Bozeman, MT, USA; Horizon Airlines operations at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport (BZN).
    • A ski vacation usually starts with a travel day.
    • Industry observers note that while free arrival-day skiing might sound too good to be true, it’s not a upcoming concept.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, november 28, 2023; Bozeman, MT, USA; Horizon Airlines operations at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport (BZN). Mandatory Credit: Joe Nicholson-Alaska Airlines (Photo: Courtesy of Alaska Airlines).

    A ski vacation usually starts with a travel day. Between catching flights, collecting luggage, and making your way to the mountains, it’s easy to lose an entire day before you ever click into your skis. But what if you could hit the slopes the same day you land, without paying for a lift ticket?

    Industry observers note that while free arrival-day skiing might sound too good to be true, it’s not a upcoming concept. Park City, Utah, previously offered a program called Quick START, which allowed travelers flying into Salt Lake City International Airport to exchange their same-day boarding pass for a complimentary lift ticket at Park City Mountain Resort, Deer Valley Resort, or Canyons Resort. Although the program has since ended, the idea of turning a travel day into a ski day hasn’t disappeared.

    Today, several ski resorts and airlines offer similar incentives. Some require flying with a specific airline, while others are available to travelers booking an eligible resort stay.

    According to recent reports, through its Atmos Rewards Alpine Getaways program, Alaska Airlines partners with ski destinations across the western United States and Canada to offer travelers special perks. For the 2026–’27 season, the airline has confirmed partnerships with Crystal Mountain in Washington and Palisades Tahoe in California, with additional resorts potentially joining as the season progresses.

    In previous seasons, the airline has also partnered with Alyeska Resort, Arctic Valley Ski Area, and Eaglecrest Ski Area in Alaska; Bogus Basin and Schweitzer in Idaho; Jackson Hole Mountain Resort in Wyoming; and Sun Peaks Resort in British Columbia.

    It has been revealed that while some participating resorts have offered complimentary lift tickets, others have provided discounted rentals and additional perks. At Palisades Tahoe, travelers can present a same-day Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines boarding pass or proof of Atmos Rewards membership to access the resort’s offer. Details for Crystal Mountain’s 2026–2’7 promotion are still being finalized.

    “Skiing is a natural fit for Alaska because we serve so many great mountain destinations across the West,” Sarah Lasky, Senior External Communications Manager at Alaska Airlines, noted.

    “Through Atmos Rewards, we want to make the journey more rewarding and connect our members with the experiences they love, including making it easier to turn the day they arrive into part of the adventure,” she continued.

    Travelers can find the latest participating resorts and offers on Alaska Airlines’ website.

    For the 2026–’27 winter season, travelers flying into Jackson Hole Airport can receive a complimentary lift ticket at one of three nearby ski resorts, regardless of which airline they choose: Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, Snow King Mountain, or Grand Targhee Resort.

    Each resort offers something slightly different. Snow King Mountain provides a full-day lift ticket, while Jackson Hole Mountain Resort and Grand Targhee offer half-day tickets. Snow King also offers night skiing on select evenings, giving travelers who arrive later in the day another opportunity to get on the mountain.

    To redeem the offer, visitors must present their boarding pass or flight confirmation showing their arrival at Jackson Hole Airport, along with a matching photo ID, at the participating resort’s ticket window.

    The complimentary ticket is only valid on the day of arrival, and blackout dates vary by resort.

    According to recent reports, for the 2026–’27 winter season, guests who reserve at least five nights of lodging through Big White Direct Bookings qualify for one free lift ticket on their arrival day. The offer is available for both upcoming and existing eligible reservations and doesn’t require flying with a particular airline. To receive the complimentary ticket, guests must present their boarding pass.

    Recent findings suggest that major White is about a 50-minute drive from Kelowna International Airport, and there is airport shuttle transportation available for those who prefer avoiding driving in the snow. For travelers arriving later in the afternoon, the resort also offers night skiing, allowing them to make use of their free ticket after dark.

    Free arrival-day skiing isn’t limited to North America. In Chile, Ski Portillo offers guests the opportunity to ski on both their arrival and departure days as part of its all-inclusive vacation packages.

    Located in the Andes Mountains beside Laguna del Inca, Ski Portillo operates during the Southern Hemisphere’s winter season, typically from June through September.

    Unlike programs that require travelers to present an airline boarding pass, Ski Portillo includes arrival and departure day skiing in its seven-night packages and three- or four-night Mini Week stays.

    It has been revealed that before booking, be mindful of your arrival time. Between collecting luggage, picking up rental equipment, and traveling from the airport to the resort, you may have less time on the mountain than expected. Booking an early flight can help maximize your ski day, while resorts offering night skiing may be better options for travelers arriving later.

    It’s also key to check blackout dates and other restrictions, as some offers are only available during certain periods of the ski season. Additionally, some resorts may require reservations or specific booking arrangements to qualify for complimentary tickets.

    In a recent development, finally, don’t forget to keep your boarding pass. Many of these programs require proof of same-day air travel, and having everything ready when you arrive can help you get on the slopes that much faster.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The 9 Best Hiking Towns to Spend Your Holidays In

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Photo: Photos from Terry's photostream via Flickr Creative Commons).
    • But not everyone can access hiking right out their front door.
    • It has been revealed that with that in mind, we’ve put together a list of the best places for hikers to holiday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: Photos from Terry's photostream via Flickr Creative Commons).

    But not everyone can access hiking right out their front door. So why not turn your holiday break into a hiking vacation? You’ll not only get to make special festive memories outside, but you can choose the geography and even the climate.

    It has been revealed that with that in mind, we’ve put together a list of the best places for hikers to holiday. Want to spend your time traipsing through deserts, among cacti and palm trees? We’ve got you covered. Looking for a more traditional experience, with snowy trails and evergreen forests? No problem. And, of course, if you like long walks on the beach and among tropical rainforests, we’ve got just the places for you.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild weather, southwestern culture, diverse landscapes, and amazing food December temps: 40-65℉ What to expect: Both desert and mountain landscapes with rocky, sandy terrain, and no snow.

    Industry observers note that for those hikers who’d rather decorate a saguaro cactus than a lodgepole pine, Tucson, Arizona is calling your name. The wildernesses around town are packed with desert flora and fauna, and crisscrossed with tons of hiking trails. This can be a tough place to explore during late spring, summer, and even into fall because it gets so scorching hot. However, in the winter, the weather is perfect for hiking, making this a prime place to spend the holidays. Beyond the trails, the food is world-renowned—Tucson has been a UNESCO City of Gastronomy for over a decade.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Fair weather, proximity to Gila National Forest and Cliff Dwellings Monument, colorful western history, and a great art scene December temps: 21-55℉ What to expect: Colder, high desert climate, with very clear weather, and tons of trails exploring the Pinos Altos and Mogollon Mountains.

    Situated on the outskirts of the Gila National Forest, Silver City is a gateway to desert hiking adventures. The Continental Divide Trail passes nearby; City of Rocks State Park is just 30 miles east of town, and the famous Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument is just 44 miles north. The monument area gets over 200 cloudless nights a year, making it a prime destination for winter stargazers. If you want a warm soak after your hikes, Faywood Hot Springs and Gila Hot Springs are both close to town.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, direct access to Zion National Park, regional access to Bryce Canyon or Grand Canyon, and a lively restaurant and art scene December temps: 30-55℉ What to expect:  A striking red sandstone desert landscape and trails both in the park and outside of it.

    In a recent development, winter is Zion National Park’s slow season, and yet it’s just as beautiful as it is any other time of year. Springdale sits just outside the park’s eastern entrance and is a prime location for a hiking holiday basecamp. Not only will you have direct access to the national park and all of its trails, but there are also worthy routes around town that don’t require an entrance fee. And if you aren’t afraid of a day trip, Bryce Canyon is 86 miles away.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, access to Lake Mead, fun holiday atmosphere, and a historic downtown December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Wide Mojave desert terrain with rolling hills and rocky mountains, canyons, panoramic lake views, and old mining and railroad infrastructure.

    The deserts of southern Nevada have a lot to offer beyond the flashing lights, casinos, and nightlife of Las Vegas. About an hour southeast of Sin City, Boulder City is a much quieter historic town that offers access to some amazing trails and outdoor recreation areas. It’s just a short drive from Boulder City to Lake Mead Recreation Area, where there are a lot of trails, walkways, and observation points. Some hikes close to town are short and approachable, while others challenge hikers with scrambles and steep climbs. The city itself is full of history; it was once an old mining town and played an important role in the Hoover Dam’s construction.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Mountain scenery and trails, access to Blue Ridge Parkway, and relatively mild temperatures and weather December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Forested mountains, waterfalls, and (potentially) snowy trails.

    Industry observers note that within minutes of Asheville, you’ll find waterfall hikes, mountain overlooks, and plenty of access to public lands. The Blue Ridge Mountains make a beautiful backdrop for town, and an even more spectacular place to explore by trail. Asheville’s thickly wooded forests are magical to hike, with trails following icy creeks and ascending ridges to spectacular views. After your hike, the town is renowned for its craft beer scene and festive holiday light displays. If a cozy Appalachian holiday is your vibe, look no further.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Situated high in the Rocky Mountains, lively restaurant and bar scene, trails in every direction, and close to two ski resorts December temps: 12-42℉ What to expect: Cold-weather mountain hikes, snowy trails, old-growth forests, and high desert terrain.

    Durango, Colorado, is a pure western mountain ski town and a genuinely cozy place to spend the holidays. The San Juan Mountains offer incredible hiking for all levels, whether you just want to stroll along a creek or climb for panoramic views of the Rockies. This region gets a lot of snow in the wintertime, so be prepared for cold weather with the right gear, knowledge, and expectations. For holiday adventurers, Durango is packed with things to do in the winter. Beyond the hiking trails, ride the historic Durango and Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad, or go skiing at Wolf Creek or Purgatory Resorts.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, subtropical winter weather, surrounded by ample inland and beach hiking, and deeply historic roots December temps: 50-70℉ What to expect: Sand dune beaches, flatland ecosystems, wetlands, and marshes.

    It has been revealed that st. Augustine offers a unique take on the traditional winter holiday. It’s coastal, subtropical, and offers landscapes and ecosystems you’ll only find in Florida—from swamp conservation areas to beach parks and historic forts. There are over 30 trails and walkways around St. Augustine, and it’s within an hour’s drive of six state parks. Most of the hiking is very approachable, following beaches, boardwalks, sand dunes, and mostly flat terrain. The town was settled over 450 years ago, so it’s also a great place for history buffs, and it annually hosts a Christmas parade and “Night of Lights” throughout December.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, tropical weather, dramatic natural scenery, laid-back island culture, and great hiking access December temps: 65-80℉ What to expect: Lush rainforests, beautiful beaches, mountains spouting waterfalls, and the opportunity to surf major swells.

    Hawaii is a famous holiday destination for obvious reasons. In the winter, the climate is pleasant; the landscape is dramatic, there are beaches a’plenty, and the hiking access is hard to beat. Waterfalls spout from the mountains, and trails wind through thick rainforest, popping out on beaches that you might have all to yourself. Hanalei, on Kauai’s North Shore, offers some of Hawaii’s best (and most diverse) hiking. Nearby are several forest reserves, Kōke’e State Park, and the Hanalei National Wildlife Refuge.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Bavarian influence, Christmas spirit, and ample winter trails to explore December temps: 15-35℉ What to expect: Snowy trails through old-growth forests and mountains, and a town that really loves to celebrate Christmas.

    Tucked away in the Cascade Mountains of Washington, along the Wenatchee River, this Bavarian-influenced town is one of the best places to spend the holidays on this list. The hiking in the surrounding mountains offers access to postcard-worthy alpine lakes, waterfalls, and ridges. It ranges from strenuous and challenging to easy and mellow. You’ll want snowshoes and/or microspikes if you blueprint on holidaying in Leavenworth, as the trails will likely be snowy and/or icy in places. The town is well-known for its Christmas zeal: It has a “Christmastown,” a Bavarian village that comes to life with live music, carols, ice carving, fireworks, and, of course, appearances by Santa Claus.

    #160675. A Very Serious Story About Falling Asleep While Belaying

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1140 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    A Very Serious Story About Falling Asleep While Belaying

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the East Face of Mount Temple, Canada, and the scene of this story's shenanigans.
    • Massive falls are commonplace while sport climbing and bouldering, but, in my opinion, the high alpine remains largely a safe space to take your brake hand off the rope.
    • This old school state of mind deeply resonated with me earlier this month on a difficult alpine climb on Mount Temple in the Canadian Rockies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the East Face of Mount Temple, Canada, and the scene of this story's shenanigans. (Photo: Mitra Samavaki / Getty).

    Massive falls are commonplace while sport climbing and bouldering, but, in my opinion, the high alpine remains largely a safe space to take your brake hand off the rope. Why? With loose rock, aerated ice, and an often minimalist rack, falling off—even with a tight belay—usually spells disaster. A climber has every reason to follow the old “the leader cannot fall” ethos.

    This old school state of mind deeply resonated with me earlier this month on a difficult alpine climb on Mount Temple in the Canadian Rockies. This 1,400-meter ice and mixed route began easily enough, with a hike up a hard-packed snow slope at 6 a.m. toward the deep cleft that marked the start. Neither my partner Rory nor I were burdened with rope management during the first hour of climbing, since our rope stayed neatly coiled in a pack.

    It has been revealed that hundreds of meters higher, below one of the crux pitches, we flaked out our rope. Above us stood a terribly skinny pillar of ice no wider than my shoulders at its base. Blue light filtered through its entirety, a sign of its youth and untrustworthiness.

    “I don’t think I should place a screw in that,” Rory decided.

    It has been revealed that I scanned the shattered quartzite behind the pillar, hoping to at least keep us attached to the mountain before Rory essentially soloed the pitch. Two nervous pitons and a shallow micro nut were all I could cobble together after 10 minutes of searching. I stomped out a waist-deep hole in the snow on the back side of the pillar and clipped into our wobbly anchor. My now four-piece anchor—plus Rory’s unshakeable climbing ability—gave us great odds of surviving his lead.

    Industry observers note that the runout pitch gave me ample opportunity to pay out slack as I pleased while munching on trail mix and rehydrating from our busy morning. After all, Rory was not allowed to fall, so he didn’t.

    Falling has been a frowned-upon practice for most of climbing’s history, especially before sport climbing became popular in the 1980s. Only relatively recently, and only in some styles of climbing, have leader falls become no longer taboo—even acceptable and encouraged.

    Sources indicate that the crusty old-timer in me knows that, in any form of free climbing, it is always safer to climb to the top of a pitch without testing your equipment, be it a skinny rope, crashpad, or ice screw. This gut instinct evolved from a time when climbing gear was not completely trustworthy. Maybe you hand-stitched your quickdraw’s webbing yourself. Maybe you’d sourced your climbing protection from a hardware store. Or maybe you had tied your lead line around your waist because drop-seat harnesses hadn’t been invented yet. In this era—really only a few decades ago—your climbing ability was the first line of defense. Ropes and harnesses and removable protection served merely as dubious back-ups.

    But the advent of regular whippers is a tragedy for one more reason: With newfangled belay devices, hang dogging, and constant pleas to “watch me,” belaying has become a real pain in the ass.

    Nearly 12 hours later, Rory and I were still on Mount Temple. We’d topped out the ice climbing portion of the face and traversed across open snow slopes and through rock bands to a final serrated crux: the Black Towers. Countless turrets of dark limestone slice across the summit ridge of Mount Temple, creating difficult route finding even on a clear summer’s day. We were approaching midnight in November and a thick fog had choked the upper mountain. Visibility hovered around 10 meters. I had no idea where we were supposed to go.

    Industry observers note that thankfully it was Rory’s lead again, and he was questing. Fifteen minutes ticked by as he wandered up a steep rocky groove, then another 15 of the rope unmoving. An hour passed. I clicked off my headlamp to save battery. More time passed. I figured I could tie off the rope and catch a few Zs, so I did. Sleep felt amazing. I was glad that even as we approached 24 hours on the move, Rory still knew the rules: The leader cannot fall. And the belayer gets to sleep.

    In a recent development, I woke up to the sound of Rory’s voice. He’d been blocked by an overhang and was downclimbing. Thick, icy fog obscured our vision as I took the rack and traversed along a snow ledge looking for easier passage. The fog would sometimes lift for an instant—I’d spot a lonely star above—and I’d frantically flick my headlamp to full strength to catch a glimpse of the mountain. But before my eyes could adjust to the upcoming sight, the fog would crash back in like a breaking wave, drowning us in uncertainty once again.

    This story does not end in a climbing success. We did not ultimately find our way through the Black Towers, nor did we share a weary, satisfied hug on the summit of Mount Temple. We became lost and a little delirious on a large mountain in the middle of the night and needed to go down.

    We stayed roped together as we retraced our steps through deep snow on the upper mountain. I was a little worried about triggering an avalanche, but mainly I was just exhausted. If I stumbled, I would prefer to slide 30 meters before being caught by the rope than well over a thousand into the next life.

    Industry observers note that rory and I regrouped at an anchor I’d built in an outcrop of yellow rock. He led out across another snowfield which terminated at a gigantic notch in an otherwise sheer ridgeline. The notch marked the start of a classic ski descent, the 60-degree Aemmer Couloir, and our escape hatch. Rory trudged toward it and I paid out rope, nodding off again.

    Suddenly, I was awake. I had not pooped all day, yet the kilogram of trail mix and sausage and cheese I’d downed was making a basement appearance.

    Industry observers note that “Rory! Do you need a real belay for this bit? I really need to poo,” I yelled into the fog.

    “No, I don’t care,” the fog yelled back.

    I let the rope feed through the anchor, then unclipped it from my belay device and, without moving even a step away from our anchor, unloaded into the snow bank.

    Industry observers note that it would have been a disgusting mess had Rory fallen and weighted the anchor, dragging me into my own steaming waste. But he didn’t, and I made it back to civilization with both my dignity and my life intact.

    Industry News: The Next Frontier of Adventure Travel Isn’t More Adventure—It’s Better Recovery. Here’s Where to Stay.

    • According to Hilton’s “The Great Rebalance: How Travelers Are Expecting to Reset and Recalibrate in 2027” survey, which surveyed 14,744 travelers across 14 countries, 65 percent of survey respondents actively book vacations that calm the body and reset the nervous system, and 79 percent say that fresh air and being outdoors help them relax when they travel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that (Photo: L to R: Four Seasons Resort Maui; Auberge Collection; Tordrillo Mountain Lodge. Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva ).

    As much as outdoor enthusiasts enjoy spending time in nature and nurturing their bodies and minds, it’s easy to lose space for rest while chasing the next thrill. But not anymore, as recent reports say travelers are consciously seeking experiences that balance adventure with restoration.

    According to Hilton’s “The Great Rebalance: How Travelers Are Expecting to Reset and Recalibrate in 2027” survey, which surveyed 14,744 travelers across 14 countries, 65 percent of survey respondents actively book vacations that calm the body and reset the nervous system, and 79 percent say that fresh air and being outdoors help them relax when they travel.

    The Global Wellness Institute’s 2026 Wellness Tourism Initiative Trends report stated that, in today’s overstimulating world, “wellness travel is increasingly shifting from performance-driven wellness toward nervous system regulation.” Booking.com noted in its 11th Annual Travel Predictions report that they expect 2027 to be the era of recovery-maxxing.

    Industry observers note that all this to say, if you’re ready to book a gorgeous getaway brimming with wellness benefits, we’re here to help. The stays on this list are a bit of a splurge, but they do include an array of rejuvenating amenities in beautiful places. (They’re listed from least to most expensive based on current room rates.) That remarked, read ahead for five U.S. destinations that ace recovery travel.

    According to recent reports, four Seasons Resort Maui at Wailea has drawn guests to its picture-perfect Wailea shores since opening in 1990 as the brand’s first tropical resort. For decades, the oceanfront resort has been world-renowned as a best-in-class property across accommodations, food, beverage, and hospitality. As of July 2026, next-gen wellness has been added to the list. With the opening of Kai Holo Spa, the resort’s warm, circadian-lit wellness sanctuary (where the lighting is built to regulate guests’ sleep-wake cycles to induce relaxation), guests are invited to zen out on island time, whether amongst the aquathermal circuit, with a Pacific Journeys massage in an open-air massage hale by the ocean, or at the adjoining Next|Health Longevity Clinic, where a hyperbaric chamber and IV therapies await.

    You can book your stay here for a minimum of $880 per night.

    Recent findings suggest that for a more landlocked wellness experience, head to Texas Hill Country to explore the expansive grounds of Canyon Ranch Austin, where a 27,000-square-foot training center and recovery lab called The Barn welcomes guests to nurture their health with the help of a gym and outdoor field. The resort also includes a sprawling 40,000-square-foot spa, making it the largest spa in Texas, that offers an array of vitality treatments, from zero-gravity neurostimulation (for improved sleep and focus) and red light beds (to reduce training fatigue and pain) to an Ammortal Chamber. The Ammortal Chamber combines both red and near-infrared light, pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy that sends electromagnetic waves through the body to ease sore muscles, molecular hydrogen, vibroacoustic sound, and guided breathwork to boost relaxation and rebalance the nervous system. Beyond that, Canyon Ranch Austin’s Women’s Wellness Collective is a dedicated women’s wellness practice that addresses hormonal therapy, brain health, sleep, perimenopause, menopause, and more.

    You can book your stay here at a minimum of $1,325 per night (per person) with the Stay Your Way package. There’s a two-night minimum stay. Unlimited meals and snacks are included, along with transportation to and from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport or Horseshoe Bay Resort Airport. With this package, you’ll also receive a $200 nightly spa and fitness credit per person. If you stay three or more nights, you’ll get a $300 health and wellness credit.

    Dunton Hot Springs is a romantic, rustic-luxe resort set in an 1800s ghost town. Nestled in Colorado’s San Juan Mountains, Dunton Hot Springs draws on its geography for its wellness offerings. The Wellness in the San Juans workshop is a guided two-hour workshop that combines breathwork, meditation, and mobility to deepen the connection between body and mind. Other ways to recover at the resort include soaking in the 85 degrees Fahrenheit to 106 degrees Fahrenheit calcium bicarbonate waters (which are meant to improve skin health and circulation) in the Bathhouse or under the stars in nature, healing sound baths, facials and massages, and individual, couple’s, and group yoga.

    In a recent development, you can book your stay here. There’s a two-night minimum stay, and rates are $1,415 per night. For example, the Echo Cabin, your most affordable option, includes a 252-square-foot cabin, mountain views, a half-bath, and a secluded outdoor shower. If you’re not in the mood to shower in nature, you’re just a short walk from the bathhouse.

    Recent findings suggest that the Lodge at Blue Sky, only minutes from Park City, approaches recovery from a different angle, leaning into energy healing and alignment. Meander through a beautiful aspen grove into The Edge Sanctuary, a luxury glamping tent where the resort’s energy healers lead intuitive energy journeys, mesmerizing sound baths, and heart-opening tea ceremonies. For a more traditional recovery experience, pop up to The Edge Spa for indulgent facials and massages overlooking Alexander Creek. The Lodge at Blue Sky guests can also invigorate their senses with contrast therapy, where heat improves circulation and cold therapy supports muscle recovery after athletic pursuits.

    You can book your stay here. Current rates start at around $1,924 per night for the 570-square-foot King Sky room, which offers one king bed, a mountain view, a 115-square-foot terrace,  and a soaking tub.

    According to recent reports, if you want to explore recovery practices without neglecting your passion for adrenaline-fueled adventure, Alaska’s Tordrillo Mountain Lodge is calling. The remote, all-inclusive luxury adventure lodge incorporates helicopters into much of its programming, from heli-skiing to the newly introduced, first-of-its-kind heli-sauna: the AlpenSauna. Earlier this year, the lodge introduced the AlpenSauna, a fly-in, custom-built sauna that the Tordrillo team moves throughout the Tordrillo Mountain Range. For example, the sauna may be positioned next to an alpine waterfall one month and in the middle of a 28-mile ice field on the Triumvirate Glacier the next. Earlier in 2026, the lodge also debuted a 2,400-square-foot wellness and recovery center co-designed by athletes, guides, and longevity experts.

    In a recent development, again, helicopter rides are baked into these experiences; the pricing isn’t cheap, so it is certainly a splurge. For a seven-night stay, the Winter package (February to April) costs $18,500 per person (or $2,643 per night). For a five-night stay with the Kings and Corn package (June), the package costs $16,000 per guest (or $3,200 per night). The least expensive stay comes in their Summer package (July to September). For instance, their “Season of the Salmon” package, which runs from August 13, 2027 to September 13, 2027, costs $10,500 per person (or $3,500 per night) for a Friday-to-Monday, three-night stay. In the summer, unlimited lodge activities include wake surfing, wakeboarding, stand-up paddleboarding, kayaking, and more.

    You can view a comprehensive list of all packages here.

    • This month, our editors backpacked the Utah desert, took in the fall foliage in the Pacific Northwest, and (finally) broke out our skis again in the Colorado mountains.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

    According to recent reports, fall often seems to happen all at once in the Front Range of Colorado: One day it’s sunny and pushing 70, the next the leaves are falling off the trees, and the day after that it’s suddenly snowing. While it can make it tough to make prepares, it also means November is a great time here for hikers who love variety.

    This month, our editors backpacked the Utah desert, took in the fall foliage in the Pacific Northwest, and (finally) broke out our skis again in the Colorado mountains. From a carbon-fiber encased power pack to a gravity filter, this gear helped us do it.

    In a recent development, of all the viral gear I’ve seen during my tenure as a Backpacker editor, the Haribo power bank had to be the funniest. At roughly 9 ounces, the 20,000mAh battery was briefly one of the lightest batteries of its capacity on the market; all of a sudden, gram-counters were scrambling to get their hands on a gadget with a smiling cartoon bear on the side.

    If you missed your chance with the Candy Battery, the NB10000 is the next best thing. At 4.94 ounces, this carbon-fiber sheathed power bank is about half the size (and half the capacity) of the Haribo one, and has a handful of nice tricks built in. Besides the standard stuff like fast charging, the NB10000 features technicolor lights built around the dual USB-C charging ports, which make it easy to find in a dark tent. At a rating of IPX7, it’s also waterproof enough to survive full immersion, making it a solid choice for paddling trips or rainy trails. One minor gripe: I found an included short USB cord handy, but it bit the dust within a few months. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief.

    This is the first fleece on the market made with Polartec’s new, hotly-anticipated second generation Alpha fabric. So what’s the big deal? Polartec claims that this new Alpha is just as warm and breathable as the older version, while being more durable and resistant to shedding. Patagonia’s pullover does feel significantly different than the old Alpha. While the underlying scaffolding looks the same, the new fabric’s texture is more like a furry shag rug than the original tufted style.

    In a recent development, over several weeks of testing, it’s proven less prone to snagging on things and disintegrating in the wash. Fit-wise, the Patagonia Pullover has a casual, boxy silhouette more meant for around town wear (a bit of an odd application for Alpha.) One caveat: The fabric weight of this pullover is quite heavy—roughly 165 GSM—compared to the usual 60-90 found on ultralight Alpha hoodies. To make a proper breathability and warmth comparison, we’ll need to wait until one of the smaller cottage brands releases a lightweight version. —Benjamin Tepler, Senior Gear Editor.

    In a recent development, when it comes to hiking fashion, I tend to care a lot more about function than form. (No shade to the backpackers out there leaning into trendy apparel; the gorpcore wave is real.) That said, it’s nice to feel good on the trail, and these pants from Skida bring a pop of pure fun to my wardrobe. Lightweight, high-waisted, and flowy, the Viska comes in five of Skida’s signature colorful prints. (If you really want to get vibrant, pair them with a matching hat or buff.) They’re both the boldest and the most comfortable pants I own; the stretch polyester/lycra blend feature a wide leg and moisture-wicking properties. Wearing them feels similar to staying in my PJs all day long, minus the fashion faux pas. With UPF 50+ protection, they’re also a good choice for scorchingly bright days.

    It has been revealed that because the fabric is so lightweight, these aren’t my go-to for actual trail miles; instead, I love to wear them lounging around camp, on long travel days, or to change into at the trailhead after a grimy hike. And I’m almost guaranteed to get a compliment or two when I wear them in public, which doesn’t hurt. —Zoe Gates, Senior Editor.

    It has been revealed that I only recently got on the gravity filter train, and it’s been a paradigm shifter for me. When I get to camp, I can fill the reservoir, hang it up, and have a faucet of filtered water at the ready. On hut trips, in the winter, it’s awesome for an extra level of filtration, removing sediment and particulates from melted, boiled snow water. The Seeker Gravity Filter in particular has really won me over. Not only can I hang it up, but it has a handle on the side that allows me to hold it and use it like a regular squeeze filter.

    It has been revealed that the filter itself is a .2 micron hollow fiber filter that’s good for up to 1,500 liters of filtered water. According to Hydrapak, it catches 99.999% of bacteria, cysts, and sediment. The specs claim it filters at a rate of one liter per minute—I feel like it’s slightly slower than that, but my filter might just need a good reverse flush. Unfortunately, the original is no longer available, so you’ll have to buy the Seeker filter kit, which includes an extra reservoir for storing your filtered water. —Will Brendza, Associate Editor.

    Patagonia Re-Tool Air Snap-T Pullover.

    Hydrapak Seeker+ 6L Gravity Filter Kit.

    #160671. Tech Report: Put Your Rock Shoes in the Oven—You’ll Thank Us

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (620 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Put Your Rock Shoes in the Oven—You’ll Thank Us

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that A pinhole image of a person peering into their oven at home.
    • According to recent reports, I grew up in a gym.
    • If there’s one thing that has held true over my years of cramming my feet into tiny, downturned rock shoes for the sake of performance, it’s that breaking in shoes sucks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A pinhole image of a person peering into their oven at home. (Photo: Getty Images).

    According to recent reports, I grew up in a gym. I learned my first curse words on a chalky, sweat-stained gym mat. I got my first tattoo with the friends I did four-by-fours with. First boyfriend, even.

    If there’s one thing that has held true over my years of cramming my feet into tiny, downturned rock shoes for the sake of performance, it’s that breaking in shoes sucks. Every time, no getting around it, a horrible experience. During one gym session, a friend said she’d pay to have someone break in her shoes for her. We were the same size, and I was pretty desperate for money at the time—but still, some things just aren’t worth it. And when you not only have to break in the shoes, but have a double training session ahead of you while your feet are screaming with pain? I’m sure that I cried once over it.

    When the pandemic hit, suddenly I wasn’t going to the gym anymore. And because—at least at the beginning—nobody was sure about transmission via holds outside, I refrained from climbing rock as well. During that turbulent time, a funny thing happened: Either my feet flattened out or my tolerance for tiny shoes decreased. Because when gyms reopened and I tried to push myself through the break-in process again, suddenly it felt a lot more hateful.

    As I complained loudly (and probably all while looking desperate) at Monkey House Carbondale in December 2020, a local friend, the pro climber Dan Mirsky, overheard me.

    “Try putting ‘em in the oven,” he said.

    Industry observers note that “No way. They’ll delaminate!” I protested.

    “No, seriously. Just for a few minutes on the lowest setting. Game-changer.”.

    Recent findings suggest that I took his tip, which I later learned he had originally gotten from another pro climber, Jonathan Siegrist, to heart. That night, I set up my station: oven, on the lowest setting (170 degrees), timer, and area on the carpet where I would dance around like a circus monkey. In the shoes went, for two minutes. I would then wear them for five to ten minutes—pacing, with some good ol’ fashioned calf raises mixed in—and then they’d go back in the oven, for another cycle or two. (Note: This only works with a standard oven, not a microwave—do not microwave your rock shoes or it will severely damage/deform them!).

    Sources indicate that I couldn’t believe the results. Those brand-new puppies felt more akin to the pair you sweated in all summer and have yet to send to a resoler (God bless the person who has to touch that pair). It was one of those moments when you realize your life has changed forever.

    According to recent reports, and a fun fact for you, which I learned with more research: Leather stretches when wet (duh!). So try the oven thing, plus adding a sprinkling of water when they shoes are still hot, prior to donning them. And voilà! Your warm, wet shoes will slide right on and stretch even more.

    According to recent reports, curious for his take, I reached out to Siegrist. “Yes, I do that sometimes!” he wrote. “Not as much any more, because I think I just simply get bigger shoes. Ha!”.

    And that, actually, might just be the best tip of all.

    According to recent reports, note: While the author has successfully applied this tip on multiple occasions, as has Siegrist and Mirsky, not all shoemakers recommend. Scarpa, for example, has noted that this method of breaking in shoes will reduce glue strength and void shoe warranty.

    #160670. “A Southern Storybook Brought to Life.” Inside South Carolina’s Luxurious Lowcountry 20,000-Acre Montage Palmetto Bluff.

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1526 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    “A Southern Storybook Brought to Life.” Inside South Carolina’s Luxurious Lowcountry 20,000-Acre Montage Palmetto Bluff.

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Photo: Top Left: Rebecca Norris; Bottom Left: Andrew Baldino; Right: Montage Palmetto Bluff).
    • Ever come across an incredible hotel that stops you mid-scroll and makes you think: Wow, wouldn’t it be something to stay there?
    • I’m traveling down a very narrow two-way road in a tinted Chevrolet Suburban when the chauffeur stops abruptly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: Top Left: Rebecca Norris; Bottom Left: Andrew Baldino; Right: Montage Palmetto Bluff).

    Ever come across an incredible hotel that stops you mid-scroll and makes you think: Wow, wouldn’t it be something to stay there? We do, too—all the time. Welcome to Friday Fantasy, where we highlight amazing hotels, lodges, cabins, tents, campsites, and other places perched in perfect outdoor settings. Read on for the intel you need to book an upcoming adventure here. Or at least dream about it.

    I’m traveling down a very narrow two-way road in a tinted Chevrolet Suburban when the chauffeur stops abruptly. He points out two alligators sunbathing on the rocks in the May River on our right. That is my first sighting of an alligator or any reptile in over 15 years—except for a strangely cute banana boa constrictor in my high school science class. I’m no fan of them.

    That gator pair, and a few more, dot the river, alongside the long road leading up to Montage Palmetto Bluff, a five-star resort in South Carolina’s Lowcountry.

    The sandy dirt road, shadowed by live oak trees draped in Spanish moss—a signature of the Lowcountry landscape—eventually opens onto the resort’s central property: a sprawling white mansion called the Main Inn.

    After the driver helps unload my bags from the truck, resort staff greet me and lead me inside across the wide porch, a hallmark of any traditional Southern residence. The dark wooden floors creak under my feet, the same kind of creaking that reminds me of walking into the comfort of my grandma’s house.

    Recent findings suggest that montage Palmetto Bluff is a 20,000-acre property tucked between Hilton Head Island and Savannah, Georgia. It has over 200 guest rooms, suites, cottages, and other residences, called Village Homes, Moreland Village Homes, and Signature Residences. (I stayed in one of the signature residences.).

    The property also offers ample outdoor and wellness activities, including a shooting club, golf course, a 13,000-square-foot spa, a lawn and racquet club, and over 20 miles of walking and biking trails.

    For folks who want to throw a lavish, intimate event or wedding, Palmetto Bluff features two beautiful chapels: the May River Chapel and the Somerset Chapel. The latter is where Justin Bieber and Hailey Baldwin held their wedding ceremony in 2019. Through the church’s arched windows, you’ll get magnificent views of the sunset.

    In a recent development, the resort is approximately a 30-minute boat ride from Daufuskie Island, a remote, bridge-free barrier island between Hilton Head Island and Savannah, Georgia. It has white-sand beaches, one paved road on the less-developed side of the island, and a rich Gullah Geechee culture. The Gullah Geechee people are descendants of enslaved West Africans who were forced to work on plantations along the southeastern coast of the United States.

    Despite the resort’s beauty, it sits atop a dark history. In the Antebellum Era, Palmetto Bluff was home to several plantations where enslaved people grew lucrative crops, including indigo, cotton, rice, corn, beans, and sweet potatoes.

    “We believe it is notable first and foremost to acknowledge the suffering endured by the enslaved individuals who lived and labored on this land,” Meghan Lamb, senior manager of marketing and public relations at Montage Palmetto Bluff, tells me. “These stories deserve to be shared openly and thoughtfully, both to honor those who came before us and to ensure their experiences, contributions, and enduring legacy are never forgotten,” she adds.

    Lamb, who walked my fellow housemates and me through much of the property and, while sharing the Bluff’s rich history, also had an excellent eye for spotting gators.

    As a Black person whose ancestors were enslaved on southern plantations, hearing about the history here was a painful reminder, but a lack of acknowledgment would have been even more so.

    During the Civil War, Union troops captured the land, and many white families and enslaved people fled the area. Wealthy bankers and businesspeople later purchased the property, and the land changed hands several times. A banker named Richard T. Wilson bought the property in 1901, expanded it, had a large mansion built on the grounds, and gave the estate its current name: “Palmetto Bluff.” The mansion burned to the ground in a 1926 fire; the ruins remain preserved on the grounds today.

    Palmetto Bluff is now owned by a private equity firm that specializes in resort management, Henderson Park and South Street Partners.

    I stayed in one of the signature residences, houses available for rent for a period of time, with three others for four days and three nights.

    The Signature Five Bedroom Lagoon Residence 1003 is a mansion with high ceilings and luxurious bathrooms, plus a fireplace, a porch, a separate cottage, and a large communal dining table nestled in the center of the home.

    According to recent reports, I chose the bedroom in the back left corner of the house; it had warm, yellow lighting, deep mahogany-colored walls, a king-sized bed, a lush en-suite bathroom, and some of the softest sheets I’ve laid my head on. Despite a packed schedule, I rested easy each night.

    You can view room rates and book your stay at a signature residence here.

    On my first night, we were welcomed with a Southern-style buffet in our signature residence. The menu was astounding: a traditional Lowcountry boil with shrimp, corn, potatoes, and sausage, plus fluffy biscuits, mac and cheese, collard greens, and peach cobbler for dessert.

    Sources indicate that there are also several places to dine across the property. Guests can indulge in fine Southern cuisine at the Octagon or at the elegant River House, which is where I ordered my first Wagyu steak. Brunch is served at Buffalos, and premium cocktails are available at Hush, a speakeasy. Along the lagoon waterway that runs through the resort is Fore & Aft, which serves delicious Mexican fare. Flame is a 1950s-vintage pizza truck you can easily walk up to and grab a slice in the evenings, Wednesday through Sunday. Buzz is a cozy cafe (I got a toasty ham-and-cheese croissant one morning that didn’t disappoint), and Melt is the Bluff’s ice cream parlor. The property even has its own gas station with a small grocery store.

    For a fun treat, you can make your own s’mores at the massive fire pit behind the Main Inn every night at 9 P.M. I did, and it brought me back to when I used to make them as a kid by the campfire in my parents’ backyard.

    Recent findings suggest that as I mentioned—my schedule was packed, but I managed to fit in a few outdoor activities. The 20-plus miles of trails on Palmetto Bluff offer scenic walking and e-biking tours.

    In a recent development, I had never been on an e-bike before, so I was pumped for this chance to do so on some beautiful trails. I liked that I could switch between regular biking and an electric boost to reach nearly 20 miles per hour. The combination of speed, wind in my hair, and stunning trail views was exhilarating, so much so that I even made the very risky decision to FaceTime my girlfriend with one hand to show her how much fun I was having.

    Andrew Baldino, the public relations and marketing coordinator at Montage Palmetto Bluff, led the e-biking tour and pointed out spots most people tend to miss. One of those, he noted, is River Road. The appeal? Sweeping live oaks, long Spanish moss, and extensive lush greenery, he tells me.

    In a recent development, the Golden Hour E-Bike Excursion lasts for one hour and 15 minutes and costs $90 per person. You can book your slot here.

    On the second day of my stay, I took a paint-and-sip class at my signature residence with renowned artist Amiri Farris, known for incorporating Gullah Geechee imagery into his work. We painted a blue crab because they’re often found in South Carolina estuaries, tidal creeks, salt marshes, and rivers.

    Recent findings suggest that on the third day, I embarked on the Daufuskie Island History Excursion tour. Because the tour lasts about four hours, you’ll need to book it early in the morning. My tour started at 7:30 A.M. It was one of the highlights of my trip. I saw dolphins along the way and learned about the island’s rich history on a golf-cart tour of the island’s untouched parts after hopping off the boat. Our captain, who steered the boat and led the golf-cart tour, made the experience even more worthwhile as he’s developed deep relationships with people on the island and shared stories about the island’s characters, bringing a humorous, jovial vibe to the trip.

    In a recent development, private tours for up to six people cost $895, tours for up to 12 people cost $1,195, and tours for up to 16 people cost $1,295. You can book them here.

    I left my trip feeling nourished, calm, and more knowledgeable about the Lowcountry than before I arrived.

    Lamb put it beautifully when I asked what about the Bluff makes visitors want to return—and even buy property on the resort: “It’s a Southern storybook brought to life.”.

    📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (306 w)

    Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

    📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (306 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, as soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins.
    • The sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part.
    • Recent findings suggest that all the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds.

    According to recent reports, as soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”.

    The sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

    Recent findings suggest that all the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential problems.

    Industry observers note that honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

    Tech Report: Search for One of the World’s Rarest Mushrooms on These Texas Trails

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that if it weren’t for Angel Schatz, the executive director at the Central Texas Mycological Society, I would have never spotted it.
    • Known as the Devil’s Cigar—or Texas Star mushroom—this curious fungi is the official mushroom of the Lone Star State.
    • Industry observers note that in addition to being geographically rare, these mushrooms tend to be exceptionally well camouflaged to their surroundings, especially in their cigar form––a dark brown bulbous lump often poking just an inch or two out of the soil with a tell-tale nipple on top.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that if it weren’t for Angel Schatz, the executive director at the Central Texas Mycological Society, I would have never spotted it. The dark brown lump of fungi was buried under leaf litter next to a blackened tree stump alongside Austin’s Shoal Creek Trail. Fortunately, locating fungi of all kinds is Schatz’s expertise. And as she led our group of mushroom-curious explorers into the trees, we all tittered with the excitement of spotting our first kirinomitake.

    Known as the Devil’s Cigar—or Texas Star mushroom—this curious fungi is the official mushroom of the Lone Star State. While it has been spotted from Lubbock to Dallas and across the border in Oklahoma (plus in Japan and Taiwan), its small geographic range makes the Texas Star a rare find. In Central Texas, it thrives on decaying cedar elm stumps.

    Industry observers note that in addition to being geographically rare, these mushrooms tend to be exceptionally well camouflaged to their surroundings, especially in their cigar form––a dark brown bulbous lump often poking just an inch or two out of the soil with a tell-tale nipple on top. They’re inedible, but locate one that has spread open into its iconic star shape (when it releases its spores with an audible hiss), and it’s hard not to get excited.

    Fortunately, there are plenty of trails in the region, especially in the Hill Country surrounding Austin and San Antonio, where you can spot this unique fungi.

    According to recent reports, to locate a Devil’s Cigar, head to areas where cedar elms grow in abundance. Scan the ground for old, black tree stumps, which mycologists refer to as “black crowns” for their blackened, multi-pointed shape.

    Industry observers note that then, get low. You may not spot them at once, especially when grass is tall or leaf litter covers the ground. Brush away any foliage and loose dirt around the stump and you may find slightly fuzzy dark brown lumps or, if you’re lucky, a tan star. Many times, two or three mushrooms grow in close proximity.

    The best time to find Devil’s Cigars in Texas is in the late fall through early spring when relative humidity is high, weather is more consistently moist, and overnight lows drop below 50°F. Head out after a rain and you’ll have an even better chance of finding them in their star form as additional moisture encourages them to crack open and send their spores flying. Once they do, you may have a week to spot them before they decompose or get nibbled by insects.

    In a recent development, want to find one for yourself? These trails offer a better-than-average opportunity.

    Devils Backbone Trail, Inks Lake State Park, Burnet.

    Distance: 3.5 miles, out-and-back.

    This short but challenging trail leads you through woods with plenty of cedar elm, up rocky spines, and alongside a creek that feeds into the lake. A bird blind at one end offers the option to identify winged creatures as well as fungi.

    Distance: 3.8 miles, out-and-back.

    Recent findings suggest that start this leisurely hike at the trailhead near Barton Springs Pool in Zilker Park near downtown Austin and head south along the Barton Creek Trail/Violet Crown Trail. Keep your eyes peeled for fungi as you hike to the 360 Trailhead, where you’ll turn around and retrace your steps.

    According to recent reports, meander through live oak and cedar elm on this quiet stretch of trail on the southern edge of San Marcos. Start at the trailhead off Hunter Road and hike Dante’s Trail, which connects with Paraiso Trail to make a loop at the end.

    #160664. Breaking: The Six Formative Moments in Every Climbing Career
